Title: Infographic Understanding Climate Change: Warmer weather not only harms human health, but agriculture and the economy have also paid the price
Content: David Nelles and Christian Serrer: Climate change has now directly or indirectly affected the lives of 7.5 billion people on the planet.  However, the impact of global warming varies from place to place, which means that people and people living together in different regions will also be affected to varying degrees.  In any case, one thing is certain: the continued warming of the climate will continue to bring all kinds of adverse effects to mankind.  Climate change can have many effects on human health, such as heat stress caused by high temperature, operating environment factors (including air temperature, humidity, wind speed and radiation heat) and clothing, and high temperature events, which can worsen heart, blood circulation and respiratory related diseases. Increase the mortality rate of these diseases.  On the other hand, high temperatures are conducive to the formation of ozone close to the ground, which has adverse effects on human health, such as may lead to decreased lung function.  Extreme weather events such as floods or storms are more frequent and can also bring more hidden risks to human health, such as injuries and even death in serious cases.  In addition, already polluted waters may increase the risk of infectious disease outbreaks due to heavy rainfall and flooding.  Another effect of climate change in Germany is the lengthening of the pollen season, which exacerbates the symptoms of respiratory diseases such as asthma or allergic rhinitis.  And such climatic conditions are more conducive to the growth and reproduction of allergenic plants, such as Ambrosia is a good example.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse Produced The 2010 increase in global deaths due to climate change A spreading vector of disease caused by climate change refers to organisms that can transmit pathogens from infected animals or humans to other animals or humans, such as ticks commonly known as ticks, or mosquitoes.  Climate change is changing the current environmental conditions in which pathogens are spread by vectors.  In recent decades, due to globalization and favorable climatic conditions, the Asian-native Aedes albopictus (also known as the Asian tiger mosquito) has reached parts of southern Europe.  In the near future, other areas of higher latitudes in Europe should also become suitable for mosquito activity due to climate change.  It is important to note that the white line mosquito spreads dengue fever and Chikungunya virus.  On the other hand, the high temperature must be maintained for a period of time before the virus can be spread through the infected mosquitoes, because the warm temperature allows the virus to successfully reproduce in the mosquitoes and then transmit the virus to humans when the mosquitoes bite.  Rising temperatures create favorable conditions for the spread of Aedes albopictus and shorten the propagation time of the virus in Aedes albopictus.  Combining globalization with the risks that come with it, such as the importation of foreign goods that could trap Aedes albopictus, or returning travelers infected with the virus, increases the risk of disease transmission.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produce Climate change impacts on agriculture High temperatures, high levels of carbon dioxide in the air, changes in rainfall patterns, and associated changing weather parameters can affect plant growth.  When the temperature rises to the most appropriate growth temperature, the yield of a particular crop can be increased, but once the temperature exceeds this optimum value, the crop yield begins to decrease.  In the case of corn and soybeans, as long as the growth period is more than 30 ° C, it is not conducive to the development of these crops.  In addition, extreme weather, especially drought and high temperatures, as well as heavy rain, can negatively affect yields. Between 2000 and 2007 alone, droughts and high temperatures have reduced global cereal crops by about 6.2%.  When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air increases, many plants respond quickly by reducing the amount of water released from the leaves and increasing photosynthesis.  In this way, there is enough water and nutrients to promote plant growth, which is known as the "CO2 fertilization effect" (CO2-Düngungseffekt).  There is debate as to how much this fertilization effect can offset the reduction in production in some areas due to changes in temperature and rainfall patterns.  In addition, increased carbon dioxide concentration in the air can promote plant growth, but it also means that the nutrient concentration in the plant will be relatively reduced.  If higher average temperatures lead to longer tillage periods, less cold damage and higher crop yields, then climate change has positive implications for higher latitudes, such as northern Europe.  In contrast, climate change is not necessarily a good thing for crop yields in tropical and subtropical regions.  Climate change comes with three different types of costs: First, the cost of damage, such as direct damage to real estate or public infrastructure caused by extreme weather events.  This is followed by adaptation costs, such as levees or ponds for flood control.  The third is the so-called avoidance costs, such as the costs of switching from fossil to renewable energy to limit future global warming.  Because it is not possible to have a clear and comprehensive picture of all the costs incurred, it is actually very difficult to calculate precise figures for the economic costs of climate change.  Therefore, the calculated cost can only depend on the assumptions made, and it is very difficult to accurately grasp the costs of such things, such as melted permafrost, so it is extremely difficult to analyze the chart below.  Photo Credit: Business Week Publishing / Produced by Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse Because of these high levels of uncertainty, it is very difficult to know exactly what climate protection measures should be taken and how much it should be interfered with from a purely economic point of view.  If people want to limit warming to 1.5 ° C, they will have to pay a very high investment cost.  Compared to setting the temperature rise range at a maximum of 3.5 ° C, the investment cost, although significantly reduced, will result in higher damage costs.  Overall, the cost of limiting global warming should be much less than the cost of damage caused by an unrestricted rise in global temperatures.  It is worth noting that as the temperature rises, the risk of irreversible damage is also increased.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse conclude that climate change is not a distant vision of the future, and that it represents more than just melting icebergs and rising sea levels, which are already threatening many people and their livelihoods.  In addition, it also shows that the temperature rise observed since the beginning of the industrial era is mainly due to man-made greenhouse gas emissions.  Fortunately, there ’ s also some ironic good news: we have the opportunity to influence the future of the climate, and we ’ re not completely powerless against climate change!  Climate model simulations show that as long as humans reduce greenhouse gas emissions, it is expected to limit the development of global warming.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produced a global average temperature forecast for greenhouse gas emissions, but since the United Nations Climate Conference (UN-Klimakonferenz) was first held in Berlin in 1995, global greenhouse gas emissions have risen by 50%, reaching a record high.  If human beings continue to produce large quantities of greenhouse gases, it is not impossible to imagine that global temperatures will rise by another 5 ° C by the end of the century.  Therefore, we must all be aware of our responsibility: how the future of the climate, and the extent to which the impact of global warming will worsen, is entirely in our hands! Title: Climate Change Impact Assessment on Taiwan ’ s Human Resources (Part I)
Content: Rising temperatures, intense heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rain are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Pixabay economic growth is engulfed if we do not make substantial and sustained global mitigation of climate change, and regional adaptation efforts, it is expected to cost us infrastructure and property, increasingly, and hinder economic growth.  In the absence of major global mitigation actions and regional adaptation efforts, rising temperatures, rising sea levels and changes in extreme weather will continue to destroy infrastructure and property, labor productivity, and community vitality, especially as regional economies and industries that rely on natural resources and climate-friendly conditions, such as agriculture, tourism, and fisheries, are increasingly vulnerable to climate change.  Rising temperatures are expected to reduce the efficiency of power generation and increase energy demand, which in turn increases the cost of electricity.  Climate change is also expected to increasingly affect trade and the economy, including import and export prices, as well as businesses with overseas operations and supply chains.  In a moderately warm world, some aspects of the economy may improve slightly in the short term.  However, if the world does not reduce greenhouse gas emissions significantly and continuously, the planet is expected to continue to warm, causing significant net damage to the economy this century, especially as adaptation efforts are thwarted.  It is expected that the annual losses in some sectors of the economy will reach hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the century, continuing to grow at the rate of past emissions.  Agriculture is highly challenged and threatened by rising temperatures, heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rains, which are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Climate change poses many challenges to maintaining and improving crop productivity, livestock health and the economic viability of rural communities.  While some regions may see gains in productivity favoring expanded or alternative crops in the coming decades, overall, production of major crops is expected to decline due to higher temperatures, potentially altering water availability, soil erosion, and outbreaks of disease and pests.  Rising temperatures during the growing season are expected to be the biggest factor in the decline in agricultural productivity.  If the temperature at night exceeds 35 ° C, it will cause rice to be unable to pollinate; it will also aggravate the impact of diseases and pests, affecting the harvest of crops; high temperature and rain will make the soil unable to maintain nutrients, reduce crop yields and increase production costs.  The expected increase in extreme hot weather is expected to result in further heat stress for livestock, resulting in significant economic losses for producers.  Climate change is also likely to cause large-scale changes in the supply and prices of many agricultural products around the world, and the global supply and prices of agricultural products will also change dramatically.  These changes threaten future gains in commodity crop production and endanger rural livelihoods.  Agricultural production is an industry that is highly dependent on natural resources such as water, soil and biodiversity.  Climate change causes global temperature increases and uneven rainfall, disrupting crop growth, affecting the original habitats of ecosystems, and affecting the yield and quality of agricultural products, endangering food security and productivity, and causing loss of biodiversity.  There are many adaptation strategies to cope with climate variability, while reversing the adverse effects of change on agricultural production.  These include changes in production content, production inputs, the adoption of new technologies, and changes in management principles.  However, these strategies have limitations under severe climate change impacts and require both long-term and short-term investments. Title: Climate change and 21% reduction in agricultural productivity
Content: In a new study led by Cornell University in the US, experts have found that farms have averaged 21 percent less yields over the past six decades as a result of climate change.  According to the researchers, this equates to a total loss of seven years of agricultural productivity growth.  Global agriculture is increasingly exposed to the effects of climate change, with warmer places such as Africa and Latin America suffering the most, and agricultural productivity growth is currently down by 34%.  To quantify the impact of human-induced climate change on what economists call “total factor productivity or a measure of overall agricultural sector productivity, ” experts developed a comprehensive econometric model.  Professor Robert Chambers, from the University of Maryland, said the results show that climate-related factors have already had a major impact on agricultural productivity.  In this paper, we used a model to estimate how the total factor productivity patterns would be if climate change were not present.  Professor Ariel Ortiz Boba, principal investigator of the study and assistant professor at Cornell University ’ s School of Applied Economics and Management, said: “We found that climate change has wiped out about seven years of progress in agricultural productivity over the past 60 years, equating to pressing the stop button for productivity growth in 2013, after which no progress has been made, and now human climate change is slowing down.  According to Professor Ortiz Boba, the group considered more than 200 systematic changes from the econometric model, and the results were largely consistent.  When we focus on different regions of the world, we find that the historical impacts of climate change have been greatest in areas that have become warmer, including areas of Africa, Latin America and Asia.  Most people see climate change as a distant problem, but it ’ s one that ’ s already having an impact.  We need to address climate change now so that we can prevent future generations from being harmed.  The study was published in the journal Nature Climate Change.  End of message.

Title: Warming continues to warm India's rainy season will expand
Content: Warming will make India ’ s summer rainy season more visible.  European studies have found that as Earth ’ s temperature gets warmer, every 1 degree Celsius increase in temperature is expected to lead to a 5% increase in summer rainfall in India, with consequences that will not only affect local crop yields in India, but also increase the chance of major flooding.  According to The Independent, India, which accounts for one fifth of the world ’ s population, relies on seasonal rains from June to September each year as a source of drinking water and farming.  However, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany found that global warming will make the rainy season stronger and more unstable.  Using 31 new climate models, the researchers analyzed possible changes in India ’ s rainy season in four future climate scenarios, including successful efforts to limit warming to 2 degrees Celsius and ineffective efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.  It was found that if we managed to keep the temperature within 2 degrees, the seasonal rainfall would increase by 10% between 1985 and 2015 by the end of the century, but if humans did nothing, the rainfall would increase by 24%.  In addition, for every 1 degree increase in global temperature, rainfall increases by 5%, compared to 3% in previous studies using earlier models.  In response to this, researcher Anders Leverman said, “As the difference becomes more pronounced from year to year, it will make the annual rainy season more unpredictable. ”  We also found that the increase in rainfall during the rainy season was more pronounced than in past climate models. ”  He also pointed out that climate change makes the rainy season more intense for many reasons, one of which is that warmer air will carry more water.  Andrew Turner, a scientist at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom, also believes that “the results also support the conclusion of earlier studies that rainfall will increase in India during the rainy season when greenhouse gases increase. ” According to CNN, India ’ s agricultural production accounts for nearly 20% of GDP, which plays an important role in the smooth development of the country.  Crops need rainfall, but too much or too little can harm plants.  In this regard, agricultural policy expert Devender Sharma pointed out that agricultural practices must adapt to climate change, but the specific way is still unknown.  “We don ’ t know how climate change will develop, and there is a possibility that a period of heavy rain will be followed by droughts or hurricanes, with no consistency, ” he said.  This will create a lot of problems for the agricultural sector and the economy, "he said.  The results of the study are published in the journal Earth Dynamics Systems.  [More details, see here]

Content: ISNA / Mazandaran, a faculty member of the Department of Agriculture of Sari University of Agricultural Sciences and Natural Resources, said: Given the occurrence of events such as climate change and climate of Mazandaran province, it is necessary to develop an optimal and appropriate cultivation model. The faculty member of the Department of Agriculture of Sari University of Agricultural Sciences and Natural Resources noted: In this optimal pattern, based on land zoning and climate change scenarios, only the places and lands planted crops will be altered and each crop will be planted in a place that has the least risk and the highest yield. Title: Climate change and water scarcity are top priorities.
Content: Assistant Professor of Water Engineering at the Faculty of Agriculture of Shahrekord University said: “The main priority of the authorities should be water shortage and climate change, so that water factories are moved to the seaside and agriculture in areas that are facing water shortage is limited. ”  He said: “It ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time.  “When we talk about climate change, we mean meteorological parameters that have been measured over long periods of time, and these changes manifest themselves in either natural or artificial forms, which are caused by humans.  Nasr Esfahani said: “Various factors such as sunspots, changes in the earth ’ s crust, changes in vegetation or the movement of continents, or changes in ocean temperature naturally cause climate change.  “What has happened in the past year is that humans have caused an imbalance in meteorological parameters due to excessive consumption of natural resources, including oil, gas and fossil fuels, and by destroying natural resources such as forests and expanding factories and cities.  The university professor pointed out that the country is climatally located in a dry region, saying: "We should not expect the climate to change from dry to wet, because this is a very wrong expectation that some in the society suggest this."  He said: "Climate change has become very clear in the last 40 years, so we have to adapt to this situation that has been fluctuating and know that drought or drought fluctuations are part of the nature of the region's climate."  Nasr Isfahani said: "In this situation, climate change is occurring and extreme phenomena such as severe droughts, drought, heat and cold are increasing, there is no alternative but to adapt to them, for example, agricultural products can be used to prevent frostbite, to use resistant products.  Regarding water resources, he said: “At the same time as the climate change, the consumption of water resources has greatly expanded, especially in the last 50 years, when agriculture has been the center of development in the country. ”  The university professor said: "If we examine the rainfall parameter in more detail, we see that the average rainfall has not changed, but the extremes have changed a lot and these changes are significant, on the other hand, the effective rainfall has not changed and the ineffective rainfall has increased, which means that there is a shortage of water resources."  He said: "What has been observed is that, contrary to the rainfall parameter, changes in the temperature parameter, especially the minimum temperature, are highly effective and the trend of increasing the minimum temperature is observed in many stations in the country."  Nasr Esfahani pointed out that in mountainous areas the precipitation has changed from solid to liquid state, adding: "When there is snow in the region, because the snow is slowly melting and sinking into underground sources, it feeds them, on the other hand, the occurrence of rain brings water runoff, which feeds surface water instead of feeding groundwater resources."  He added that excessive consumption of water resources, expansion of the area under cultivation, non-observance of the cultivation pattern and the use of traditional methods for irrigation have led to the reduction of groundwater.  Assistant Professor of Water Engineering at Shahrekord University emphasized: "The authorities were aware of the current situation, but they did not think that the effects of climate change would be egregious and misrepresented, and today we face a fundamental problem, for example, if there was a shortage of water, it was solved by harvesting from underground water resources and we assigned this problem to the future."  He continued: “We have reached a point where groundwater resources are not the answer to the shortage of water, and this problem has become such that measures must be taken.  Nasr Esfahani said that for short-term purposes, water resources have not been considered because steel and water mills have been built in the country, which if this decision process continues, despite the lack of water resources, will still be built in the future.  “We should not expect that one day our country will be as abundant as Europe, because the lack of rainfall in our region has been caused by the rotation of the earth and the circulation of the atmosphere, so in addition to adapting to climate change, if there is to be a cost to this, it should be done today and we should not postpone those costs to the future, because we may face more limitations in the future. ”  The university professor noted that the main priority of the authorities should be water scarcity and climate change, so that water factories are moved to the seaside and agriculture is limited in areas with water scarcity.  End of message.

Title: Land abuse contributes to climate change
Content: The land is often abused and contributes to the harm of climate change 2019-08-06 16: 42 Taiwan Awakening News reporter Zhuang Ruimeng / Taipei reported that the land has been used by humans to cultivate and lose its original function of absorbing carbon.  (Photo by M. Prinke on Flicker under Creative Commons license) Share Facebook Treating land better helps humanity fight climate change.  The UN Intergovernmental Panel of Experts on Climate Change, which is currently meeting, will present an updated report on the current state of human land use.  Experts pointed out that due to human behavior, land has changed from carbon capture to carbon release, threatening to exacerbate the power of climate change, and highlighting the importance of land use.  According to The Independent, global soils can currently absorb 1% of carbon, down from 7% in the past.  If the land is cultivated in a more sustainable way, carbon will be absorbed by the soil to become a carbon reservoir.  Currently, 1 / 3 of all pollution emissions come from land.  “If we take the severity of the climate problem seriously now, it will be worse if we don ’ t have land as a carbon reservoir, ” said Li Wen, a representative of the World Resources Institute. The scientists also pointed out that continued pressure on land, including the provision of food, wood and plant raw materials to meet increasing population needs, will make carbon reduction targets more difficult to achieve.  In addition, 33% of arable land has been used to grow crops that provide animal feed.  Professor Lixon of the University of Clanfield in the UK also believes that the latest IPCC report will provide more evidence that land degradation will also exacerbate climate change and lead to an increase in the crisis.  Addressing land abuse can focus on intensive agriculture, which involves farming on as small a land as possible, allowing more natural land to absorb carbon dioxide, according to the BBC.  Another option is to farm in a less dense and friendly climate.  Either way, however, the IPCC report will point out that poor farmers will be the group most affected by global warming.  Professor Berman, of the University of Oxford ’ s Institute of Environmental Change, said climate change had led to soil erosion in the south of the UK through more intense rainfall.  “Warmer temperatures and heavier rainfall will worsen soil erosion, soil compaction, loss of organic matter and biodiversity, and soil and rock flows, ” said Li Huicheng, chairman of the IPCC.“ I hope this report will serve to remind the world more about the threat that climate change poses to land. ”  [More details, see here]

Content: David Nelles and Christian Serrer: Climate change has now directly or indirectly affected the lives of 7.5 billion people on the planet.  However, the impact of global warming varies from place to place, which means that people and people living together in different regions will also be affected to varying degrees.  In any case, one thing is certain: the continued warming of the climate will continue to bring all kinds of adverse effects to mankind.  Climate change can have many effects on human health, such as heat stress caused by high temperature, operating environment factors (including air temperature, humidity, wind speed and radiation heat) and clothing, and high temperature events, which can worsen heart, blood circulation and respiratory related diseases. Increase the mortality rate of these diseases.  On the other hand, high temperatures are conducive to the formation of ozone close to the ground, which has adverse effects on human health, such as may lead to decreased lung function.  Extreme weather events such as floods or storms are more frequent and can also bring more hidden risks to human health, such as injuries and even death in serious cases.  In addition, already polluted waters may increase the risk of infectious disease outbreaks due to heavy rainfall and flooding.  Another effect of climate change in Germany is the lengthening of the pollen season, which exacerbates the symptoms of respiratory diseases such as asthma or allergic rhinitis. Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produce Climate change impacts on agriculture High temperatures, high levels of carbon dioxide in the air, changes in rainfall patterns, and associated changing weather parameters can affect plant growth.  When the temperature rises to the most appropriate growth temperature, the yield of a particular crop can be increased, but once the temperature exceeds this optimum value, the crop yield begins to decrease.  In the case of corn and soybeans, as long as the growth period is more than 30 ° C, it is not conducive to the development of these crops.  In addition, extreme weather, especially drought and high temperatures, as well as heavy rain, can negatively affect yields. Between 2000 and 2007 alone, droughts and high temperatures have reduced global cereal crops by about 6.2%.  When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air increases, many plants respond quickly by reducing the amount of water released from the leaves and increasing photosynthesis.  In this way, there is enough water and nutrients to promote plant growth, which is known as the "CO2 fertilization effect" (CO2-Düngungseffekt).  There is debate as to how much this fertilization effect can offset the reduction in production in some areas due to changes in temperature and rainfall patterns.  In addition, increased carbon dioxide concentration in the air can promote plant growth, but it also means that the nutrient concentration in the plant will be relatively reduced.  If higher average temperatures lead to longer tillage periods, less cold damage and higher crop yields, then climate change has positive implications for higher latitudes, such as northern Europe.  In contrast, climate change is not necessarily a good thing for crop yields in tropical and subtropical regions.  Climate change comes with three different types of costs: First, the cost of damage, such as direct damage to real estate or public infrastructure caused by extreme weather events.  This is followed by adaptation costs, such as levees or ponds for flood control.  The third is the so-called avoidance costs, such as the costs of switching from fossil to renewable energy to limit future global warming.  Because it is not possible to have a clear and comprehensive picture of all the costs incurred, it is actually very difficult to calculate precise figures for the economic costs of climate change. Compared to setting the temperature rise range at a maximum of 3.5 ° C, the investment cost, although significantly reduced, will result in higher damage costs. Agriculture is highly challenged and threatened by rising temperatures, heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rains, which are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Climate change poses many challenges to maintaining and improving crop productivity, livestock health and the economic viability of rural communities.  While some regions may see gains in productivity favoring expanded or alternative crops in the coming decades, overall, production of major crops is expected to decline due to higher temperatures, potentially altering water availability, soil erosion, and outbreaks of disease and pests.  Rising temperatures during the growing season are expected to be the biggest factor in the decline in agricultural productivity.  If the temperature at night exceeds 35 ° C, it will cause rice to be unable to pollinate; it will also aggravate the impact of diseases and pests, affecting the harvest of crops; high temperature and rain will make the soil unable to maintain nutrients, reduce crop yields and increase production costs.  The expected increase in extreme hot weather is expected to result in further heat stress for livestock, resulting in significant economic losses for producers.  Climate change is also likely to cause large-scale changes in the supply and prices of many agricultural products around the world, and the global supply and prices of agricultural products will also change dramatically.  These changes threaten future gains in commodity crop production and endanger rural livelihoods.  Agricultural production is an industry that is highly dependent on natural resources such as water, soil and biodiversity.  Climate change causes global temperature increases and uneven rainfall, disrupting crop growth, affecting the original habitats of ecosystems, and affecting the yield and quality of agricultural products, endangering food security and productivity, and causing loss of biodiversity.  There are many adaptation strategies to cope with climate variability, while reversing the adverse effects of change on agricultural production.  These include changes in production content, production inputs, the adoption of new technologies, and changes in management principles.  However, these strategies have limitations under severe climate change impacts and require both long-term and short-term investments.  High risk to health Climate change Air quality and health risks from extreme weather, air quality, and insects and pests, diseases transmitted through food and water supplies, are increasingly threatening the health and well-being of already vulnerable people; changes in temperature and precipitation increase air quality and health risks from wildfires (or incineration) and ground ozone pollution; rising air and water temperatures and more intense extreme weather are expected to increase exposure to waterborne diseases and foodborne diseases (food Sexual diseases), affecting the safety of food and water supplies.  Due to climate change, the frequency and severity of allergic diseases, including asthma and pollen fever, are expected to increase.  It also changes and expands the geographical distribution of disease-carrying insects and pests, exposing more people to the lice that bring Lyme disease and the mosquitoes that transmit Zika virus (such as dengue, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and Nile virus), which affect different transregions.  For example, communities in southwestern Taiwan are particularly vulnerable to the combined health effects of vector-borne diseases and high temperatures and floods.  Extreme and climate-related weather can have lasting mental health effects on communities, with adverse consequences, in particular resulting in degradation of livelihoods or relocation of communities.  Including the elderly, children, people in low-income communities and some indigenous and new communities, they tend to be disproportionately affected by the health impacts of climate change and are less resilient.  This helps individuals, communities, and counties to prepare for climate change risks with policies and programs to adapt and mitigate to reduce the number of injuries, illnesses, and deaths from adverse health outcomes.  According to the study, if the average temperature in Taiwan increases by 1 ° C in the future, the high risk of dengue fever will increase to 86, affecting more than 7 million people. In addition, the number of medium-risk areas has also increased to 203, and the future warming status will significantly increase the prevalence of dengue fever in Taiwan.  In addition, the increase in temperature in Taiwan will also increase the risk of related infectious diseases, and the impact of rainfall changes on infectious diseases will be more significant when the "daily extreme rainfall" is greater than 200mm.  In the face of the impact of climate change on public health, the adaptation that must be considered and prepared can be classified as at least three major aspects of infectious diseases, chronic non-communicable diseases and emergency medical care.  The main adjustment policies can basically be considered from the angle of strengthening and prevention.

Title: Climate change and 21% reduction in agricultural productivity
Content: In a new study led by Cornell University in the US, experts have found that farms have averaged 21 percent less yields over the past six decades as a result of climate change.  According to the researchers, this equates to a total loss of seven years of agricultural productivity growth.  Global agriculture is increasingly exposed to the effects of climate change, with warmer places such as Africa and Latin America suffering the most, and agricultural productivity growth is currently down by 34%.  To quantify the impact of human-induced climate change on what economists call “total factor productivity or a measure of overall agricultural sector productivity, ” experts developed a comprehensive econometric model.  Professor Robert Chambers, from the University of Maryland, said the results show that climate-related factors have already had a major impact on agricultural productivity.  In this paper, we used a model to estimate how the total factor productivity patterns would be if climate change were not present.  Professor Ariel Ortiz Boba, principal investigator of the study and assistant professor at Cornell University ’ s School of Applied Economics and Management, said: “We found that climate change has wiped out about seven years of progress in agricultural productivity over the past 60 years, equating to pressing the stop button for productivity growth in 2013, after which no progress has been made, and now human climate change is slowing down.  According to Professor Ortiz Boba, the group considered more than 200 systematic changes from the econometric model, and the results were largely consistent.  When we focus on different regions of the world, we find that the historical impacts of climate change have been greatest in areas that have become warmer, including areas of Africa, Latin America and Asia.  Most people see climate change as a distant problem, but it ’ s one that ’ s already having an impact.  We need to address climate change now so that we can prevent future generations from being harmed.  The study was published in the journal Nature Climate Change.  End of message.

Title: Warming continues to warm India's rainy season will expand
Content: Warming will make India ’ s summer rainy season more visible.  European studies have found that as Earth ’ s temperature gets warmer, every 1 degree Celsius increase in temperature is expected to lead to a 5% increase in summer rainfall in India, with consequences that will not only affect local crop yields in India, but also increase the chance of major flooding.  According to The Independent, India, which accounts for one fifth of the world ’ s population, relies on seasonal rains from June to September each year as a source of drinking water and farming.  However, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany found that global warming will make the rainy season stronger and more unstable.  Using 31 new climate models, the researchers analyzed possible changes in India ’ s rainy season in four future climate scenarios, including successful efforts to limit warming to 2 degrees Celsius and ineffective efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.  It was found that if we managed to keep the temperature within 2 degrees, the seasonal rainfall would increase by 10% between 1985 and 2015 by the end of the century, but if humans did nothing, the rainfall would increase by 24%.  In addition, for every 1 degree increase in global temperature, rainfall increases by 5%, compared to 3% in previous studies using earlier models.  In response to this, researcher Anders Leverman said, “As the difference becomes more pronounced from year to year, it will make the annual rainy season more unpredictable. ”  We also found that the increase in rainfall during the rainy season was more pronounced than in past climate models. ”  He also pointed out that climate change makes the rainy season more intense for many reasons, one of which is that warmer air will carry more water.  Andrew Turner, a scientist at the University of Reading in the United Kingdom, also believes that “the results also support the conclusion of earlier studies that rainfall will increase in India during the rainy season when greenhouse gases increase. ” According to CNN, India ’ s agricultural production accounts for nearly 20% of GDP, which plays an important role in the smooth development of the country.  Crops need rainfall, but too much or too little can harm plants.  In this regard, agricultural policy expert Devender Sharma pointed out that agricultural practices must adapt to climate change, but the specific way is still unknown.  “We don ’ t know how climate change will develop, and there is a possibility that a period of heavy rain will be followed by droughts or hurricanes, with no consistency, ” he said.  This will create a lot of problems for the agricultural sector and the economy, "he said.  The results of the study are published in the journal Earth Dynamics Systems.  [More details, see here]

Title: In the North Caucasus and southern Russia will increase snowfall and droughts
Content: Climatologists predict that in the 21st century, the amount and intensity of snowfall will increase throughout Russia, and in some regions, arid conditions are expected to worsen.  This is reported by RIA Novosti with reference to the national report “Global climate and soil cover of Russia: assessment of risks and environmental and economic consequences of land degradation ”.  The study was conducted with the aim of developing measures for adapting agricultural and forest management systems and technologies to climate change.  Discussion of the report, analyzing the forecast scenarios of climate change and their impact on agriculture and forestry, was held at the Vasily Dokuchaev Soil Institute.  According to scientists, if at the beginning of the XXI century in Russia there was a small increase in precipitation, then by the middle of the century it will increase, especially in the eastern and northern regions of the country.  “The increase in summer precipitation is most significant, mainly in the north and east of Russia.  In the south of the European part of Russia - in the Southern and North Caucasus Federal Districts - the worsening of arid (on average per year) conditions is expected, "the study says.  At the same time, more "sharp" precipitation will probably occur in the form of separate showers or snowfalls.  There will also be more floods and floods.  Note that recently, scientists said that in 30 years the climate of the Rostov region in 30 years may change to subtropical, and the weather on the coast of the Sea of Azov will be close to the climate of Abkhazia and Sochi.  So far, we are lagging behind in temperatures: in the subtropics, the annual is + 11, we have + 9.95, - said Lyudmila Bespalova, Doctor of Geographical Sciences.  In her opinion, the summer shallowing of the Don in 2017, when the water left the coast by ten meters, is one of the brightest examples of climate change.  Changes in climatic conditions can lead not only to a change in flora and fauna, but also to a change in the economy of the region.  For example, Don farmers will have to breed new varieties of wheat and shift the timing of crops.

Title: Climate change and water scarcity are top priorities.
Content: Assistant Professor of Water Engineering at the Faculty of Agriculture of Shahrekord University said: “The main priority of the authorities should be water shortage and climate change, so that water factories are moved to the seaside and agriculture in areas that are facing water shortage is limited. ”  He said: “It ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time.  “When we talk about climate change, we mean meteorological parameters that have been measured over long periods of time, and these changes manifest themselves in either natural or artificial forms, which are caused by humans.  Nasr Esfahani said: “Various factors such as sunspots, changes in the earth ’ s crust, changes in vegetation or the movement of continents, or changes in ocean temperature naturally cause climate change.  “What has happened in the past year is that humans have caused an imbalance in meteorological parameters due to excessive consumption of natural resources, including oil, gas and fossil fuels, and by destroying natural resources such as forests and expanding factories and cities.  The university professor pointed out that the country is climatally located in a dry region, saying: "We should not expect the climate to change from dry to wet, because this is a very wrong expectation that some in the society suggest this."  He said: "Climate change has become very clear in the last 40 years, so we have to adapt to this situation that has been fluctuating and know that drought or drought fluctuations are part of the nature of the region's climate."  Nasr Isfahani said: "In this situation, climate change is occurring and extreme phenomena such as severe droughts, drought, heat and cold are increasing, there is no alternative but to adapt to them, for example, agricultural products can be used to prevent frostbite, to use resistant products.  Regarding water resources, he said: “At the same time as the climate change, the consumption of water resources has greatly expanded, especially in the last 50 years, when agriculture has been the center of development in the country. ”  The university professor said: "If we examine the rainfall parameter in more detail, we see that the average rainfall has not changed, but the extremes have changed a lot and these changes are significant, on the other hand, the effective rainfall has not changed and the ineffective rainfall has increased, which means that there is a shortage of water resources."  He said: "What has been observed is that, contrary to the rainfall parameter, changes in the temperature parameter, especially the minimum temperature, are highly effective and the trend of increasing the minimum temperature is observed in many stations in the country."  Nasr Esfahani pointed out that in mountainous areas the precipitation has changed from solid to liquid state, adding: "When there is snow in the region, because the snow is slowly melting and sinking into underground sources, it feeds them, on the other hand, the occurrence of rain brings water runoff, which feeds surface water instead of feeding groundwater resources."  He added that excessive consumption of water resources, expansion of the area under cultivation, non-observance of the cultivation pattern and the use of traditional methods for irrigation have led to the reduction of groundwater.  Assistant Professor of Water Engineering at Shahrekord University emphasized: "The authorities were aware of the current situation, but they did not think that the effects of climate change would be egregious and misrepresented, and today we face a fundamental problem, for example, if there was a shortage of water, it was solved by harvesting from underground water resources and we assigned this problem to the future."  He continued: “We have reached a point where groundwater resources are not the answer to the shortage of water, and this problem has become such that measures must be taken.  Nasr Esfahani said that for short-term purposes, water resources have not been considered because steel and water mills have been built in the country, which if this decision process continues, despite the lack of water resources, will still be built in the future.  “We should not expect that one day our country will be as abundant as Europe, because the lack of rainfall in our region has been caused by the rotation of the earth and the circulation of the atmosphere, so in addition to adapting to climate change, if there is to be a cost to this, it should be done today and we should not postpone those costs to the future, because we may face more limitations in the future. ”  The university professor noted that the main priority of the authorities should be water scarcity and climate change, so that water factories are moved to the seaside and agriculture is limited in areas with water scarcity.  End of message.

Title: Land abuse contributes to climate change
Content: The land is often abused and contributes to the harm of climate change 2019-08-06 16: 42 Taiwan Awakening News reporter Zhuang Ruimeng / Taipei reported that the land has been used by humans to cultivate and lose its original function of absorbing carbon.  (Photo by M. Prinke on Flicker under Creative Commons license) Share Facebook Treating land better helps humanity fight climate change.  The UN Intergovernmental Panel of Experts on Climate Change, which is currently meeting, will present an updated report on the current state of human land use.  Experts pointed out that due to human behavior, land has changed from carbon capture to carbon release, threatening to exacerbate the power of climate change, and highlighting the importance of land use.  According to The Independent, global soils can currently absorb 1% of carbon, down from 7% in the past.  If the land is cultivated in a more sustainable way, carbon will be absorbed by the soil to become a carbon reservoir.  Currently, 1 / 3 of all pollution emissions come from land.  “If we take the severity of the climate problem seriously now, it will be worse if we don ’ t have land as a carbon reservoir, ” said Li Wen, a representative of the World Resources Institute. The scientists also pointed out that continued pressure on land, including the provision of food, wood and plant raw materials to meet increasing population needs, will make carbon reduction targets more difficult to achieve.  In addition, 33% of arable land has been used to grow crops that provide animal feed.  Professor Lixon of the University of Clanfield in the UK also believes that the latest IPCC report will provide more evidence that land degradation will also exacerbate climate change and lead to an increase in the crisis.  Addressing land abuse can focus on intensive agriculture, which involves farming on as small a land as possible, allowing more natural land to absorb carbon dioxide, according to the BBC.  Another option is to farm in a less dense and friendly climate.  Either way, however, the IPCC report will point out that poor farmers will be the group most affected by global warming.  Professor Berman, of the University of Oxford ’ s Institute of Environmental Change, said climate change had led to soil erosion in the south of the UK through more intense rainfall.  “Warmer temperatures and heavier rainfall will worsen soil erosion, soil compaction, loss of organic matter and biodiversity, and soil and rock flows, ” said Li Huicheng, chairman of the IPCC.“ I hope this report will serve to remind the world more about the threat that climate change poses to land. ”  [More details, see here]

passages.title: Berlinale ends with Iranian film victory
passages.passage: The 70th Berlin Festival ended with the triumph of the Iranian drama "There is No Evil Here" directed by Mohammad Rasoulof - an almanac of four novels about the degrees of human freedom, about the problems of painful moral choice in the most difficult circumstances.  A scene from the movie "There's No Evil Here."  Photo: Cosmopol Film / provided by the press service of the Berlin Festival The film won the main prize of the Berlinale - "Golden Bear".  The hall applauded standing, many cried: the director could not personally receive the award - for political reasons, he was forbidden to travel outside the country.  This decision of the jury was perceived as a sign of solidarity with the disgraced master.  The Grand Prix of the jury was awarded to the drama of American Eliza Hittman with a complex title "Never rarely sometimes always" - about a girl from Pennsylvania, who, accompanied by a cousin, goes to New York to secretly from her parents to have an abortion.  The best director recognized Korean Hong Sansu, presented in the competition "The woman who ran away" - he received the "Silver Bear".  For the best female role of the "Silver Bear" received Paula Beer for the film "Undine" (Germany), the best actor was named Italian Elio Germano, who played the artist-primitivist of the first half of the twentieth century Antonio Ligabue in the biopic "I wanted to hide".  The best screenplay was considered "Bad Tales" by the D'Innocenzo brothers (Italy).  "Silver Bear" for outstanding artistic contribution was awarded to the German cameraman Jürgen Jürges, who shot the films of the project "Dow".  The award, established in honor of the 70th anniversary of the festival - another "Silver Bear" was crowned by the Franco-Belgian comedy of the digital age "Delete the history" directed by Benoit Delepin and Gustave Kerverne.

passages.title: Winners of the 2019 Berlin Festival are announced
passages.passage: According to the Mehr News Agency, the Berlin Film Festival recognized its winners an hour ago when it presented its main prize to the illegal representative of Iranian cinema.  Iranian cinema had four official representatives at the event, but the new film, Mohammad Rasoulof, which was produced in Iran without legal process and sent to the festival, was given special attention by the organizers of the event.  The Berlin Film Festival has previously paid more attention to the unofficial representatives of Iranian cinema and even anti-Iranian works.  According to Variety, the winners of the Silver and Gold Bears were announced on Saturday at the closing ceremony of the 70th Berlin Film Festival.  The International Competition Jury Awards were awarded: Golden Bear for Best Picture: Mohammad Rasoulof of The Great Jury Prize Silver Bear: “Never, Rarely, Sometimes, Always ” Eliza Hitman of USA Silver Bear Award Best Director: Hong Sang-soo for“ The Woman Who Escaped ” South Korea Silver Bear Award: Paula Bear Winner for “Ondyne ” Director Christian Petzold of Germany Award for Best Screenplay Winner Silver Bear: Elio Germano for“ Hidden ” Giorgio Dieretti of Italy Award for Best Screenplay Winner Silver Bear: Damiano and Fabio Dinochenzo for “Bad Stories ” Special Prize 70th Berlinale Silver Bear Winner:“ Eliminate Histori ” directed by Benoit Delpin and Gustave Croerne of France and Belgium Best Outstanding Artistic Achievement Silver Bear Winner: Jerogen Yorgis for Filming “Dao.Natasha ” by Ilya Kezhanovsky and Ekaterina Ortel (Germany) Best First Film:“ The Magrha ” by Camilo Risterpo Best Documentary Feature: “Exposure to the Radiation ” Directed by Rieti Pan Award Best Short Film Gold Bear:“ T ” by Keisha Ray Witherspoon Jury Award Winner Silver Bear Award Winner: "Filipino" by Rafael Manuel Uday Short Film Award: "Lucy the Genius" by Adrien Marizou Fipreschi Jury also won the award in the international competition section to "Ondin" directed by Christian Petzold.  The Panorama Award went to Bassam Tariq's "Joker Mongol" and won the award in the Forum section "Twentieth Century" directed by Matthew Rankin.  In the Panorama Audience category, Father, directed by Serdan Golabowicz, was selected as the winner of the Fiction Film Award.  In the same section, the second award was given to “Feel Not Hard ” directed by Faraz Shariat and the third award was given to“ Hope ” directed by Maria Sudal.  In the 2020 documentary section, the first prize was awarded to David France ’ s “Welcome to Chechnya ”, while the second prize was awarded to Susan Regina Moyers ’“ Saudi Escape ” and the third to “Little Girl ” by Sebastian Lifshitz of France.  In the jury section of the World Church, the international competition section award was given to “The Devil Does Not Exist ” by Mohammad Rasoulof and won the Panorama section“ Father ” by Serdan Golabovich from Serbia.  The film "Saudi Escape" by Swiss director Suzanne Regina Moyers was also praised. passages.title: The End of Berlinale: Women ’ s Full Hands and Iranians ’ Empty Hands
passages.passage: The Berlin International Film Festival ended on Saturday, February 24 with a special ceremony.  The ceremony was attended by more than 1,600 guests at Berlin ’ s Berlinale Palace.  The Best Golden Bear Award went to the Romanian film “Don ’ t Touch Me ” by Adina Pintielli.  Iranian filmmakers returned home empty-handed this time.  In the main section of this year ’ s festival, 24 films were screened, of which 19 were competing for the Golden Bear and the Silver Bears of Berlinale.  This year ’ s jury consisted of German director and producer Tom Tikor, American critic Stephanie Zachark, Spanish film expert Chema Prado, American producer Adele Romanski, Japanese actress and musician Ryuichi Sakamoto, and Belgian actor Cecil de France.  “Don ’ t Touch Me ” co-directed by Germany, France, Romania, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic won the Berlinale Golden Bear.  The film also won the festival ’ s 50,000 Euro prize as the first film.  The Grand Jury Prize went to Polish film Mogue, and the Silver Bear went to American director Wes Anderson for his film Island of Dogs.  Other awards in this year ’ s main section were awarded in the following order: Silver Bear for Best Actor: Anthony Bajon for his performance in Praying from France.  Silver Bear for Best Actress: Anna Brown for her role in the film Heir Women from Paraguay.  (The film, directed by Marcelo Martisi, also received the Silver Bear Award for Best Film with a New Vision.)  Silver Bear for Best Screenplay: Alonso Virilassius and Manuel Alcala from Mexico for Museum Film.  Silver Bear for Outstanding Art Work: Elena Okinaya from Russia for the costume design of the Dolatov film.  The best short and documentary films in the Golden Bear category were given to the Rwandan and Swiss short film The Men Behind the Wall, directed by Samuel Eichmore, from Israel and the Silver Bear, and to the Rwandan and Swiss short film Imfura.  In the documentary category, Ruth Beckermann ’ s “Waltz Waldheim ” from Austria was selected as the best film of the year for the Berlinale.  The other Berlinale Awards are held annually in Berlinale, another section entitled Panorama.  In this section, awards are given to the best films by audience selection.  This year, the film "Profile", directed by Timur Bekmantov, and the documentary "Silence of Others", directed by Almodeena Karasedo, were awarded in the Panorama category.  The profile is a joint creation of the United States, Russia, Britain and Cyprus and the silence of others is a joint product of the United States and Spain.  The Crystal Bear received the adolescents section over the age of 14 from the Swiss feature film "Fortona" by Germinal Rao.  The film also won the 7,500 Euro International Jury Prize.  In this section, the film "Kim Hollikhanda" by Sara Voltmaier from the Netherlands was also awarded the Crystal Bear and the film Dressage by Pouya Badkoobeh was honored.  In the “Generation ” category for children ’ s films, this year the feature film“ Hand on Heart ” by Luke Picard from Canada and the short film “Guide to a 12-year-old Girl ” by Tilda Cobham Hervey from Australia received the Crystal Bears.  The empty hands of Iranians and the audacity of Leila Hatami all the Iranian artists present at the Berlin International Film Festival returned home empty-handed this year, and only the film “Dresaj ” directed by Pooya Badkoobeh was appreciated for the clever narrative of the story.  But the press conference of Mani Haghighi and Leila Hatami, the director and lead actress of the film "Pig", created controversy.  At the press conference, Leila Hatami lamented that peaceful protests in Iran are being violently suppressed, saying she suffered greatly from the issue.  In contrast, Mani Haghighi, while acknowledging that there is censorship in Iran and that artists are trying to circumvent this censorship in their own way, protested to journalists why they always ask political questions at press conferences when they reach Iranian artists instead of doing their work.  After the conference, Leila Hatami was severely criticized by the Fajr Film Festival officials and some regime figures on social media.  But Mani Haghighi supported Hatami in a video posted on YouTube and social media, saying: “Peaceful demonstrations are people ’ s natural right and they should not be repressed for it.  Laila Hatami ’ s discomfort was justified, and I understand that. ”

Title: The End of Berlinale: Women ’ s Full Hands and Iranians ’ Empty Hands
Content: The Berlin International Film Festival ended on Saturday, February 24 with a special ceremony.  The ceremony was attended by more than 1,600 guests at Berlin ’ s Berlinale Palace.  The Best Golden Bear Award went to the Romanian film “Don ’ t Touch Me ” by Adina Pintielli.  Iranian filmmakers returned home empty-handed this time.  In the main section of this year ’ s festival, 24 films were screened, of which 19 were competing for the Golden Bear and the Silver Bears of Berlinale.  This year ’ s jury consisted of German director and producer Tom Tikor, American critic Stephanie Zachark, Spanish film expert Chema Prado, American producer Adele Romanski, Japanese actress and musician Ryuichi Sakamoto, and Belgian actor Cecil de France.  “Don ’ t Touch Me ” co-directed by Germany, France, Romania, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic won the Berlinale Golden Bear.  The film also won the festival ’ s 50,000 Euro prize as the first film.  The Grand Jury Prize went to Polish film Mogue, and the Silver Bear went to American director Wes Anderson for his film Island of Dogs.  Other awards in this year ’ s main section were awarded in the following order: Silver Bear for Best Actor: Anthony Bajon for his performance in Praying from France.  Silver Bear for Best Actress: Anna Brown for her role in the film Heir Women from Paraguay.  (The film, directed by Marcelo Martisi, also received the Silver Bear Award for Best Film with a New Vision.)  Silver Bear for Best Screenplay: Alonso Virilassius and Manuel Alcala from Mexico for Museum Film.  Silver Bear for Outstanding Art Work: Elena Okinaya from Russia for the costume design of the Dolatov film.  The best short and documentary films in the Golden Bear category were given to the Rwandan and Swiss short film The Men Behind the Wall, directed by Samuel Eichmore, from Israel and the Silver Bear, and to the Rwandan and Swiss short film Imfura.  In the documentary category, Ruth Beckermann ’ s “Waltz Waldheim ” from Austria was selected as the best film of the year for the Berlinale.  The other Berlinale Awards are held annually in Berlinale, another section entitled Panorama.  In this section, awards are given to the best films by audience selection.  This year, the film "Profile", directed by Timur Bekmantov, and the documentary "Silence of Others", directed by Almodeena Karasedo, were awarded in the Panorama category.  The profile is a joint creation of the United States, Russia, Britain and Cyprus and the silence of others is a joint product of the United States and Spain.  The Crystal Bear received the adolescents section over the age of 14 from the Swiss feature film "Fortona" by Germinal Rao.  The film also won the 7,500 Euro International Jury Prize.  In this section, the film "Kim Hollikhanda" by Sara Voltmaier from the Netherlands was also awarded the Crystal Bear and the film Dressage by Pouya Badkoobeh was honored.  In the “Generation ” category for children ’ s films, this year the feature film“ Hand on Heart ” by Luke Picard from Canada and the short film “Guide to a 12-year-old Girl ” by Tilda Cobham Hervey from Australia received the Crystal Bears.  The empty hands of Iranians and the audacity of Leila Hatami all the Iranian artists present at the Berlin International Film Festival returned home empty-handed this year, and only the film “Dresaj ” directed by Pooya Badkoobeh was appreciated for the clever narrative of the story.  But the press conference of Mani Haghighi and Leila Hatami, the director and lead actress of the film "Pig", created controversy.  At the press conference, Leila Hatami lamented that peaceful protests in Iran are being violently suppressed, saying she suffered greatly from the issue.  In contrast, Mani Haghighi, while acknowledging that there is censorship in Iran and that artists are trying to circumvent this censorship in their own way, protested to journalists why they always ask political questions at press conferences when they reach Iranian artists instead of doing their work.  After the conference, Leila Hatami was severely criticized by the Fajr Film Festival officials and some regime figures on social media.  But Mani Haghighi supported Hatami in a video posted on YouTube and social media, saying: “Peaceful demonstrations are people ’ s natural right and they should not be repressed for it.  Laila Hatami ’ s discomfort was justified, and I understand that. ”

Title: The End of Berlinale: Women ’ s Full Hands and Iranians ’ Empty Hands
Content: The Berlin International Film Festival ended on Saturday, February 24 with a special ceremony.  The ceremony was attended by more than 1,600 guests at Berlin ’ s Berlinale Palace.  The Best Golden Bear Award went to the Romanian film “Don ’ t Touch Me ” by Adina Pintielli.  Iranian filmmakers returned home empty-handed this time.  In the main section of this year ’ s festival, 24 films were screened, of which 19 were competing for the Golden Bear and the Silver Bears of Berlinale.  This year ’ s jury consisted of German director and producer Tom Tikor, American critic Stephanie Zachark, Spanish film expert Chema Prado, American producer Adele Romanski, Japanese actress and musician Ryuichi Sakamoto, and Belgian actor Cecil de France.  “Don ’ t Touch Me ” co-directed by Germany, France, Romania, Bulgaria and the Czech Republic won the Berlinale Golden Bear.  The film also won the festival ’ s 50,000 Euro prize as the first film.  The Grand Jury Prize went to Polish film Mogue, and the Silver Bear went to American director Wes Anderson for his film Island of Dogs.  Other awards in this year ’ s main section were awarded in the following order: Silver Bear for Best Actor: Anthony Bajon for his performance in Praying from France.  Silver Bear for Best Actress: Anna Brown for her role in the film Heir Women from Paraguay.  (The film, directed by Marcelo Martisi, also received the Silver Bear Award for Best Film with a New Vision.)  Silver Bear for Best Screenplay: Alonso Virilassius and Manuel Alcala from Mexico for Museum Film.  Silver Bear for Outstanding Art Work: Elena Okinaya from Russia for the costume design of the Dolatov film.  The best short and documentary films in the Golden Bear category were given to the Rwandan and Swiss short film The Men Behind the Wall, directed by Samuel Eichmore, from Israel and the Silver Bear, and to the Rwandan and Swiss short film Imfura.  In the documentary category, Ruth Beckermann ’ s “Waltz Waldheim ” from Austria was selected as the best film of the year for the Berlinale.  The other Berlinale Awards are held annually in Berlinale, another section entitled Panorama.  In this section, awards are given to the best films by audience selection.  This year, the film "Profile", directed by Timur Bekmantov, and the documentary "Silence of Others", directed by Almodeena Karasedo, were awarded in the Panorama category.  The profile is a joint creation of the United States, Russia, Britain and Cyprus and the silence of others is a joint product of the United States and Spain.  The Crystal Bear received the adolescents section over the age of 14 from the Swiss feature film "Fortona" by Germinal Rao.  The film also won the 7,500 Euro International Jury Prize.  In this section, the film "Kim Hollikhanda" by Sara Voltmaier from the Netherlands was also awarded the Crystal Bear and the film Dressage by Pouya Badkoobeh was honored.  In the “Generation ” category for children ’ s films, this year the feature film“ Hand on Heart ” by Luke Picard from Canada and the short film “Guide to a 12-year-old Girl ” by Tilda Cobham Hervey from Australia received the Crystal Bears.  The empty hands of Iranians and the audacity of Leila Hatami all the Iranian artists present at the Berlin International Film Festival returned home empty-handed this year, and only the film “Dresaj ” directed by Pooya Badkoobeh was appreciated for the clever narrative of the story.  But the press conference of Mani Haghighi and Leila Hatami, the director and lead actress of the film "Pig", created controversy.  At the press conference, Leila Hatami lamented that peaceful protests in Iran are being violently suppressed, saying she suffered greatly from the issue.  In contrast, Mani Haghighi, while acknowledging that there is censorship in Iran and that artists are trying to circumvent this censorship in their own way, protested to journalists why they always ask political questions at press conferences when they reach Iranian artists instead of doing their work.  After the conference, Leila Hatami was severely criticized by the Fajr Film Festival officials and some regime figures on social media.  But Mani Haghighi supported Hatami in a video posted on YouTube and social media, saying: “Peaceful demonstrations are people ’ s natural right and they should not be repressed for it.  Laila Hatami ’ s discomfort was justified, and I understand that. ”

passages.title: Four refugees, including two children, drowned in the English Channel.
passages.passage: Four asylum-seekers, including two children, drowned in the English Channel (Reuters) Photo source: A rescue operation has been going on for hours by French boats since French authorities announced the deaths of two children and a man and woman who were trying to cross the English Channel to reach Britain.  A boat carrying refugees has sunk across the English Channel between France and Britain.  The prosecutor of the French city of Dunkirk has opened an investigation into the cause of the sinking of the ship.  These people are said to be Iranian.  A massive rescue operation has been under way for hours, which crashed near the northern French city of Dunkirk.  According to French authorities, two children aged 5 and 8 and a man and woman died.  The other 14 were taken to hospitals in the port of Calais and the French city of Dunkirk.  The English Channel, between France and Britain, is one of the world ’ s busiest waterways, and it can be dangerous to cross by small vessels, especially in winter when the sea is stormy.  Another disaster came after the British Meteorological Office warned of bad weather and strong winds in the Channel region.  Natalie Alpeik, MP for the Dover region in the British Parliament, said: “It ’ s terrible that there ’ s been another disaster on the canal.  Human traffickers have no respect for human life: "A sailboat accidentally encountered a ship and alerted French authorities of the incident.  Four French ships, a Belgian helicopter and a French fishing vessel were involved in the rescue.  Since the beginning of the year, more than 7,400 asylum seekers have arrived in Britain by sea in small boats.  While there are still two months left until the end of 2020, that number is 1,825 more than in 2019.  The survivors were taken by helicopter to hospitals in the port of Calais and the northern French city of Dunkirk on Thursday, August 6, and a total of 235 migrants, including several pregnant women, crossed the English Channel from Europe to the southern coast of Britain.  This is the highest recorded number of illegal immigrants arriving in the region in a single day.  About ten days ago, Home Secretary Priti Patel announced the “most significant revision ” of the country ’ s asylum system in a decade.

passages.passage: “Men don ’ t have hearts. ”  An Iranian refugee waiting in France to somehow enter Britain told reporters they are looking at the English Channel these days, where he has taken four members of an Iranian family of five from us and has not returned the body of their 15-month-old baby.  The rescue team, released the day after a boat sank in the English Channel, said the boat left the coast at 9: 30 a.m. after authorities and weather officials had warned earlier that the weather was not suitable for the boats.  Reports vary as to the number of people on board; some sources say the sinking boat had 19 people on board, and some say there were 28 people on board, Iranian and Iraqi.  After the accident, a number of helicopters, military boats and fishing boats approached to help people who were drowning.  The coast of Dunkirk, north of France and the country ’ s closest coast to Britain, is known as one of the main illegal crossings from France to Britain.  In addition to the French police and navy, NGOs are patrolling these not-too-deep but extremely turbulent waters on a daily basis to rescue refugees who are desperate for water.  Rescue teams were not close enough to do anything faster on Wednesday after a boat accident.  A French rescue helicopter in the port of Dunkirk, Rasoul Irannejad, 35, the father of a Kurdish family from Sardasht, West Azerbaijan, died before being pulled out of the water, his wife Shiva Mohammad Panahi, 35, and two children, Anita, 9, and Armin, 6, died after being pulled out of the water, and their 15-month-old baby Artin has not yet been found.  French officials say John is unlikely to be a slave.  Mr. Irannejad ’ s brother, the uncle of the drowned children, says the family left Iran in the summer.  They criticized his father ’ s simple labor income and everything he had and didn ’ t have, and they went illegally to Turkey, from there to Italy.  After a 20-day stay in Italy, they arrived in France.  Their destination was the UK, and twice before the final attempt by sea, they tried to cross the border illegally and enter the UK, where they thought they would earn £100 a day and pay back the loans they had taken and be happy.  A friend of the Irannejad family, who was with them in France, said about their decision to cross the Channel: “About a month ago, we talked about it with Shiva.  "I told him it was very dangerous and if something happened, the kids..."  The family friend, who asked the Guardian to be called Ali, said Shiva replied, “Everyone goes the same way, God willing, nothing happens. ”  Immigration laws have been tightened in recent months in the UK.  Under the impact of the coronavirus epidemic, safe routes to enter and declare asylum in the country have been closed, but small boats and the English Channel are still open.  So far this year, at the end of the 10th month of 2020, 7,400 people have made their way to the UK via the English Channel, four times the number of people who entered the UK illegally last year.  At least seven people have drowned in these waters this year, including four members of Mr. Irannejad ’ s family, as well as their missing baby.  The cost of crossing the Channel for refugees is between 5,000 and 6,000 euros per person.  Getting out of Iran, especially if you live in border areas, doesn ’ t cost much.  The main cost is to pass through Turkey and get to one of the Western European countries.  In the case of the Irannejad family, crossing the Turkish waters to Italy and arriving from Italy to France amounted to almost 8,000 euros per person.  At least €13,000 for every person from Turkey until they reach the UK.  This number needs to be multiplied by five to find out what the Iranian family, apart from their lives, has paid for taking refuge in another country.  The tent on the right: the last residence of the “Irannejad ” family in the past three days after the last incident of the sinking of the refugee boat in the English Channel, in addition to Boris Johnson, other British officials have also expressed regret about the incident and promised to cooperate with the French authorities to clarify the dimensions of the incident, but at the same time they have not opened the legal route of refugees to their country.  Following Wednesday ’ s incident, UNHCR has expressed hope that Britain will open legal pathways for refugees to prevent a repeat of the tragedy, although even if such a decision is made in the coming days, the Irannejad family will no longer be returned to us.  Those who leave the country to seek asylum, in the first step, burn their ID documents such as passports, national ID cards and identity cards and prefer to live without the country for a while, rather than find shelter elsewhere through a path that was very dangerous even in ordinary days and became more difficult during the coronavirus epidemic.  Refugees often escape war, chaos, political conflicts and socio-economic crises.  Some of them clash with the central governments of their country and flee because of political charges, some flee because of threats of murder and assault from the chaos and conflict of armed groups and civil war, and some seek a place where they can feed themselves and their families more safely.  The fear of conflict with the police due to participation in ordinary crimes, fraud, return checks, interference in smuggling and theft, and the like sometimes causes people to cross the borders of countries illegally and apply for asylum.  There are those who, in the hope of heaven, go elsewhere, without knowing what the hell it is to live in a camp, to be detained in a temporary detention center before receiving a residence permit in the host country, and how dangerous and even deadly the road can be. Each has a story.  Last year, we did a detailed local search for actors for the children ’ s roles in the movie Walnut Tree.  The children should have spoken the Kurdish language of Sorani, which is the language and accent of Sardasht people.  Only a few Iranian cities in the north of Kurdistan and the south of West Azerbaijan speak this particular dialect, which made it difficult.  One of the roles we were looking for was the role of a six-year-old girl in the film.  Look at the girl in the second photo, her eyes.  It is a combination of pain and at the same time beauty and hope.  This girl was one of our final few options, along with a few other beautiful and innocent girls, each of whom came to us with the hope that they might find a future for themselves by flaunting their talents for a few who came from Tehran. What a strange name! He has also stated that foreigners are advertising Utopia to Iranian citizens abroad.
