Title: What is the origin of the food crisis in Latin America?
Content: According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) website, the Latin American and Caribbean region produces enough food to meet the needs of all its inhabitants.  So the main problem with hunger in the region is not the lack of food, but the obstacles and difficulties faced by the poor to obtain it.  FAO Deputy General and Representative of the Organization for Latin America Julio Bardege told DW on the occasion of World Food Day that hunger in Latin America is due to insufficient income and significant economic inequality, which afflicts millions of people in the region.  According to a new report by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), food prices remained high for a seventh consecutive month in the last month of 2020, with dairy products and vegetable oils driving the biggest price increases.  According to the FAO, the rise in food prices was due to higher demand and weaker dollar values.  According to experts, although there is no pressure on food shortages, the impact of the epidemic on the supply chain and the restriction of traffic has caused damage to farms.  Latin America and the Caribbean, which produce more than 14 percent of the world ’ s food, are also looking to reshape their farming arrangements to feed 10 billion people by 2050.  However, the COVID-19 epidemic has caused an unprecedented setback in the region ’ s struggle against hunger, adding more than 20 million people to the ranks of poverty.  The unprecedented health crisis that has plagued the world for nearly two years has also hit Latin America.  Latin America, which was among the most vulnerable regions in the world due to the epidemic, has seen the spread of poverty and food shortages in recent decades, not only due to the spread of the coronavirus and the increase in deaths caused by it, but also due to numerous other factors such as climate change, mismanagement and the increasing deterioration of the labor market and sanctions.  The epidemic puts 45 million people in Latin America in a state of absolute poverty.  A situation that has sounded warnings and alarms about the lack of social security networks to reduce the consequences of the epidemic in Latin America.  The NGO Action Against Hunger reported a three-fold increase in the number of people suffering from food insecurity in Latin America in 2020 due to the outbreak of COVID-19.  In Peru, 80 percent of people lost their jobs or their incomes dropped by an average of 33 percent, according to the Humanitarian Institute ’ s survey.  The 20% drop in global food production due to climate change is another crisis that experts have warned of.  Studies show that climate change has reduced global food production by more than 20 percent in the past 60 years.  Farmers have one-fifth less food than they had in 1961; in warmer regions such as Latin America and Africa, the decline is up to 34 percent.  According to available data, the United States only sees growth of 5 to 15 percent, while the world's population is projected to reach 10 billion by 2050.  Climate change has changed the favorable conditions for growing crops and is hurting the food chain in the future.  Experts believe that temperature in plant growth and development is one of the important factors.  Temperature, along with the surface of light; carbon dioxide, temperature humidity, water and nutrients, affect the growth and ultimately the production of crops.  All of these factors need to be balanced.  While the global population continues to rise, a new study suggests that agricultural productivity has fallen sharply due to the effects of climate change.  On the other hand, some coercive measures by the hegemonic powers against the countries of the Latin American resistance, such as Venezuela, have exacerbated the food crisis in the region.  Along with mismanagement of the country ’ s food security, the impact of sanctions has affected 96 percent of Venezuelans, according to a new study.  The region ’ s response to the epidemic of the Director General of the Latin American Regional Agricultural Organization has increased despite the region ’ s worsening agricultural export unemployment during the epidemic.  In response to COVID-19 pandemic, the director of the Food and Agriculture Organization has sought to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of food production with a strategic approach, and has made a huge change in the agricultural sector with new regional initiatives.  The senior official of the agricultural organization of the region also emphasized the need for large-scale investments, especially in supply chain infrastructure and agricultural innovations, expressed hope about the region ’ s significant capacities, such as the enormous natural resources of the region, abundance of fresh water and fertile lands, as well as diverse ecosystems.  Despite this, the devastating effects of the epidemic will continue to plague the Latin American region.  Predictably, in most of these countries, rising debt due to the injection of emergency funds into the health sector and the provision of direct assistance to affected families and industrial sectors affected by the recession reduced economic activity by 7.7% in 2020.  The unemployment rate, which is the main cause of poverty, increased by 2.6 percent and with a significant portion of the workforce leaving, it reached 10.7 percent from its previous year in 2019.  In the same vein, because it was not possible for many jobs to work remotely, only 21.3 percent of those employed in the Latin American region were able to continue working this way.  According to the study, the highest unemployment rate was found in Peru (39.5%), Argentina (20.9%), Colombia (21.8%), Costa Rica (20.1%), and in the poorest households, informal work dominated.  According to the website Wordo Mitters, more than 33,581 million people in Latin America and the Caribbean have been infected with the coronavirus, and more than 1.2 million people have died from the disease.

Title: Infographic Understanding Climate Change: Warmer weather not only harms human health, but agriculture and the economy have also paid the price
Content: David Nelles and Christian Serrer: Climate change has now directly or indirectly affected the lives of 7.5 billion people on the planet.  However, the impact of global warming varies from place to place, which means that people and people living together in different regions will also be affected to varying degrees.  In any case, one thing is certain: the continued warming of the climate will continue to bring all kinds of adverse effects to mankind.  Climate change can have many effects on human health, such as heat stress caused by high temperature, operating environment factors (including air temperature, humidity, wind speed and radiation heat) and clothing, and high temperature events, which can worsen heart, blood circulation and respiratory related diseases. Increase the mortality rate of these diseases.  On the other hand, high temperatures are conducive to the formation of ozone close to the ground, which has adverse effects on human health, such as may lead to decreased lung function.  Extreme weather events such as floods or storms are more frequent and can also bring more hidden risks to human health, such as injuries and even death in serious cases.  In addition, already polluted waters may increase the risk of infectious disease outbreaks due to heavy rainfall and flooding.  Another effect of climate change in Germany is the lengthening of the pollen season, which exacerbates the symptoms of respiratory diseases such as asthma or allergic rhinitis.  And such climatic conditions are more conducive to the growth and reproduction of allergenic plants, such as Ambrosia is a good example.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse Produced The 2010 increase in global deaths due to climate change A spreading vector of disease caused by climate change refers to organisms that can transmit pathogens from infected animals or humans to other animals or humans, such as ticks commonly known as ticks, or mosquitoes.  Climate change is changing the current environmental conditions in which pathogens are spread by vectors.  In recent decades, due to globalization and favorable climatic conditions, the Asian-native Aedes albopictus (also known as the Asian tiger mosquito) has reached parts of southern Europe.  In the near future, other areas of higher latitudes in Europe should also become suitable for mosquito activity due to climate change.  It is important to note that the white line mosquito spreads dengue fever and Chikungunya virus.  On the other hand, the high temperature must be maintained for a period of time before the virus can be spread through the infected mosquitoes, because the warm temperature allows the virus to successfully reproduce in the mosquitoes and then transmit the virus to humans when the mosquitoes bite.  Rising temperatures create favorable conditions for the spread of Aedes albopictus and shorten the propagation time of the virus in Aedes albopictus.  Combining globalization with the risks that come with it, such as the importation of foreign goods that could trap Aedes albopictus, or returning travelers infected with the virus, increases the risk of disease transmission.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produce Climate change impacts on agriculture High temperatures, high levels of carbon dioxide in the air, changes in rainfall patterns, and associated changing weather parameters can affect plant growth.  When the temperature rises to the most appropriate growth temperature, the yield of a particular crop can be increased, but once the temperature exceeds this optimum value, the crop yield begins to decrease.  In the case of corn and soybeans, as long as the growth period is more than 30 ° C, it is not conducive to the development of these crops.  In addition, extreme weather, especially drought and high temperatures, as well as heavy rain, can negatively affect yields. Between 2000 and 2007 alone, droughts and high temperatures have reduced global cereal crops by about 6.2%.  When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air increases, many plants respond quickly by reducing the amount of water released from the leaves and increasing photosynthesis.  In this way, there is enough water and nutrients to promote plant growth, which is known as the "CO2 fertilization effect" (CO2-Düngungseffekt).  There is debate as to how much this fertilization effect can offset the reduction in production in some areas due to changes in temperature and rainfall patterns.  In addition, increased carbon dioxide concentration in the air can promote plant growth, but it also means that the nutrient concentration in the plant will be relatively reduced.  If higher average temperatures lead to longer tillage periods, less cold damage and higher crop yields, then climate change has positive implications for higher latitudes, such as northern Europe.  In contrast, climate change is not necessarily a good thing for crop yields in tropical and subtropical regions.  Climate change comes with three different types of costs: First, the cost of damage, such as direct damage to real estate or public infrastructure caused by extreme weather events.  This is followed by adaptation costs, such as levees or ponds for flood control.  The third is the so-called avoidance costs, such as the costs of switching from fossil to renewable energy to limit future global warming.  Because it is not possible to have a clear and comprehensive picture of all the costs incurred, it is actually very difficult to calculate precise figures for the economic costs of climate change.  Therefore, the calculated cost can only depend on the assumptions made, and it is very difficult to accurately grasp the costs of such things, such as melted permafrost, so it is extremely difficult to analyze the chart below.  Photo Credit: Business Week Publishing / Produced by Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse Because of these high levels of uncertainty, it is very difficult to know exactly what climate protection measures should be taken and how much it should be interfered with from a purely economic point of view.  If people want to limit warming to 1.5 ° C, they will have to pay a very high investment cost.  Compared to setting the temperature rise range at a maximum of 3.5 ° C, the investment cost, although significantly reduced, will result in higher damage costs.  Overall, the cost of limiting global warming should be much less than the cost of damage caused by an unrestricted rise in global temperatures.  It is worth noting that as the temperature rises, the risk of irreversible damage is also increased.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse conclude that climate change is not a distant vision of the future, and that it represents more than just melting icebergs and rising sea levels, which are already threatening many people and their livelihoods.  In addition, it also shows that the temperature rise observed since the beginning of the industrial era is mainly due to man-made greenhouse gas emissions.  Fortunately, there ’ s also some ironic good news: we have the opportunity to influence the future of the climate, and we ’ re not completely powerless against climate change!  Climate model simulations show that as long as humans reduce greenhouse gas emissions, it is expected to limit the development of global warming.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produced a global average temperature forecast for greenhouse gas emissions, but since the United Nations Climate Conference (UN-Klimakonferenz) was first held in Berlin in 1995, global greenhouse gas emissions have risen by 50%, reaching a record high.  If human beings continue to produce large quantities of greenhouse gases, it is not impossible to imagine that global temperatures will rise by another 5 ° C by the end of the century.  Therefore, we must all be aware of our responsibility: how the future of the climate, and the extent to which the impact of global warming will worsen, is entirely in our hands! Title: Tyumen scientists conduct observations at the biological station "Lake Kuchak"
Content: Tyumen scientists conduct observations at the biological station "Lake Kuchak" | Photo: Tyumen State University | Photo: Tyumen State University Regular observations of the growth and development of various field crops, taking into account the impact on plants of meteorological factors on the experimental site of the biological station of Tyumen State University "Lake Kuchak" are carried out by scientists of the Institute of Biology of Tyumen State University since May 2020, according to the Department of Strategic Communications of the university.  The territory is a natural testing ground for the study of ecological plasticity of plants and the selection of forms with high adaptive potential.  As explained by the head of the Department of Botany, Biotechnology and Landscape Architecture of Tyumen State University, Professor Nina Bome, the growing season of 2020 is characterized by an extremely uneven distribution in time of precipitation and air temperature.  Drought-resistant forms of cultivated plants that have the ability to adapt to the temperature stresses of the environment acquire practical value.  The success of the introduction of cultivated species can be achieved only with the right selection of varieties and the development of elements of regional cultivation technology.  In this regard, plant forms created by scientists of the Institute of Biology with the help of modern genetic and biotechnological methods are of particular value: chemical mutagenesis, hybridization, selection.  In total, about 800 experimental variants of the genetic diversity of cultivated plants were included in the research.  Some research projects are carried out in partnership with scientific and educational Russian and foreign centers.

Title: Climate Change Impact Assessment on Taiwan ’ s Human Resources (Part I)
Content: Rising temperatures, intense heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rain are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Pixabay economic growth is engulfed if we do not make substantial and sustained global mitigation of climate change, and regional adaptation efforts, it is expected to cost us infrastructure and property, increasingly, and hinder economic growth.  In the absence of major global mitigation actions and regional adaptation efforts, rising temperatures, rising sea levels and changes in extreme weather will continue to destroy infrastructure and property, labor productivity, and community vitality, especially as regional economies and industries that rely on natural resources and climate-friendly conditions, such as agriculture, tourism, and fisheries, are increasingly vulnerable to climate change.  Rising temperatures are expected to reduce the efficiency of power generation and increase energy demand, which in turn increases the cost of electricity.  Climate change is also expected to increasingly affect trade and the economy, including import and export prices, as well as businesses with overseas operations and supply chains.  In a moderately warm world, some aspects of the economy may improve slightly in the short term.  However, if the world does not reduce greenhouse gas emissions significantly and continuously, the planet is expected to continue to warm, causing significant net damage to the economy this century, especially as adaptation efforts are thwarted.  It is expected that the annual losses in some sectors of the economy will reach hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the century, continuing to grow at the rate of past emissions.  Agriculture is highly challenged and threatened by rising temperatures, heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rains, which are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Climate change poses many challenges to maintaining and improving crop productivity, livestock health and the economic viability of rural communities.  While some regions may see gains in productivity favoring expanded or alternative crops in the coming decades, overall, production of major crops is expected to decline due to higher temperatures, potentially altering water availability, soil erosion, and outbreaks of disease and pests.  Rising temperatures during the growing season are expected to be the biggest factor in the decline in agricultural productivity.  If the temperature at night exceeds 35 ° C, it will cause rice to be unable to pollinate; it will also aggravate the impact of diseases and pests, affecting the harvest of crops; high temperature and rain will make the soil unable to maintain nutrients, reduce crop yields and increase production costs.  The expected increase in extreme hot weather is expected to result in further heat stress for livestock, resulting in significant economic losses for producers.  Climate change is also likely to cause large-scale changes in the supply and prices of many agricultural products around the world, and the global supply and prices of agricultural products will also change dramatically.  These changes threaten future gains in commodity crop production and endanger rural livelihoods.  Agricultural production is an industry that is highly dependent on natural resources such as water, soil and biodiversity.  Climate change causes global temperature increases and uneven rainfall, disrupting crop growth, affecting the original habitats of ecosystems, and affecting the yield and quality of agricultural products, endangering food security and productivity, and causing loss of biodiversity.  There are many adaptation strategies to cope with climate variability, while reversing the adverse effects of change on agricultural production.  These include changes in production content, production inputs, the adoption of new technologies, and changes in management principles.  However, these strategies have limitations under severe climate change impacts and require both long-term and short-term investments.  High risk to health Climate change Air quality and health risks from extreme weather, air quality, and insects and pests, diseases transmitted through food and water supplies, are increasingly threatening the health and well-being of already vulnerable people; changes in temperature and precipitation increase air quality and health risks from wildfires (or incineration) and ground ozone pollution; rising air and water temperatures and more intense extreme weather are expected to increase exposure to waterborne diseases and foodborne diseases (food Sexual diseases), affecting the safety of food and water supplies.  Due to climate change, the frequency and severity of allergic diseases, including asthma and pollen fever, are expected to increase.  It also changes and expands the geographical distribution of disease-carrying insects and pests, exposing more people to the lice that bring Lyme disease and the mosquitoes that transmit Zika virus (such as dengue, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and Nile virus), which affect different transregions.  For example, communities in southwestern Taiwan are particularly vulnerable to the combined health effects of vector-borne diseases and high temperatures and floods.  Extreme and climate-related weather can have lasting mental health effects on communities, with adverse consequences, in particular resulting in degradation of livelihoods or relocation of communities.  Including the elderly, children, people in low-income communities and some indigenous and new communities, they tend to be disproportionately affected by the health impacts of climate change and are less resilient.  This helps individuals, communities, and counties to prepare for climate change risks with policies and programs to adapt and mitigate to reduce the number of injuries, illnesses, and deaths from adverse health outcomes.  According to the study, if the average temperature in Taiwan increases by 1 ° C in the future, the high risk of dengue fever will increase to 86, affecting more than 7 million people. In addition, the number of medium-risk areas has also increased to 203, and the future warming status will significantly increase the prevalence of dengue fever in Taiwan.  In addition, the increase in temperature in Taiwan will also increase the risk of related infectious diseases, and the impact of rainfall changes on infectious diseases will be more significant when the "daily extreme rainfall" is greater than 200mm.  In the face of the impact of climate change on public health, the adaptation that must be considered and prepared can be classified as at least three major aspects of infectious diseases, chronic non-communicable diseases and emergency medical care.  The main adjustment policies can basically be considered from the angle of strengthening and prevention.

Title: Eric Firvald, Syngenta. “Climate change will be a major global factor ”
Content: — More than two years ago, we met at SPIEF — shortly after the closing of the deal with ChemChina.  You said then that this is the optimal shareholder, which will preserve the independence of the company, including the operating one.  It's been a while.  Can you say the same now?  I would like to draw your attention to the fact that outside of China the influence of our shareholders is quite limited.  The only thing they can do is support us, including investment.  Support is coming!  We have made five acquisitions, including our largest acquisition of Nidera, the digital platform Cropio, two deals in the vegetable segment and one in the digital tools segment.  There is also support from shareholders.  Let ’ s say in China, they help us to better understand the local market in order to improve the service of Chinese customers.  Historically, there have been problems in China with the use of low-quality pesticides, overuse of pesticides, low-quality fertilizers...  As a result, this has led to soil degradation and environmental problems.  Accordingly, with the new Chinese shareholder, we have the opportunity to increase our share in the Chinese market, while bringing our high-quality modern products to it and thereby help the country overcome the difficulties that it has. - How has your share in the Chinese market increased since the transaction? - We have significantly increased it.  We had less than 1% of the market in China and 6% in the crop.  By the end of last year, we already had 4% for seeds and 10% of the crop protection market.  If we talk about the implementation, then by the end of 2019, our sales in China amounted to $336 million.  By the end of 2020, our sales in China will exceed $4 billion, and the market share will increase significantly.  Eric Firvald.  CEO Syngenta was born on July 29, 1959 in the United States.  1981 – Graduated from the University of Delaware (Chemical Engineering).  1998 — studied in the program of training of top managers of Harvard Business School.  2003 - Vice President, Agriculture and Nutrition, DuPont Group.  2008 — Chairman of the Board of Directors, President and CEO at Nalco (water treatment technologies, services for energy companies).  2011 — President of EcoLab (water, hygiene and energy technologies and services).  2012 — Executive Director of Univar (world distributor of chemical products, including agricultural products).  Since 2016 — CEO of Syngenta. — Tell us the details of the transactions. — Nidera is a company that deals with corn and soybean seeds, one of the largest players of this level in Brazil and Argentina.  And, of course, integration with the Syngenta business turns the now merged company Syngenta-Nidera into one of the leading market makers in the markets of these countries.  With the acquisition of Nidera, we also gained access to advanced technologies in the field of sunflower and, by the way, these technologies will soon be available in Russia.  The second two important acquisitions are the digital platforms Cropio and Strider.  Digital platforms help to keep a record of the use of all those crop protection products and fertilizers used by the agricultural producer, and give him certain advice.  In this way, they help us to improve our customer service.  Among our deals are two more seed companies in the vegetable segment: Abbott & Cobb and Floranova.  These companies are mainly represented in the markets of the United States and the United Kingdom, but their hermoplasm is used far beyond these countries. – Name, if possible, the amount of each of the transactions. – This I can not do.  I will only say that all five acquisitions cost the company and its shareholders $2 billion. — Can an M & A deal similar to one of these five be concluded in Russia? — I will say at once that Chinese investors fully support our course to increase investment in Russian business.  But here we have a few other plans.  When I talk about Russia, I mean, first of all, not M & A, but the construction of a plant for the production of plant protection products near Lipetsk and the creation of the Institute for Seed Protection in the Voronezh region, which will support our business in this segment.  We also intend to significantly increase the number of full-time employees in Russia. - And how much does Russia occupy in your sales? - 4%, but at the same time we maintain a constant increase in sales here.  Of course, its pace is not as fast as in China, but our starting positions in the two countries are different. – Another question about the new digital assets of Syngenta.  The Cropio platform is relatively known in Russia, and almost nothing is known about Strider.  What is this platform where it works, what is its uniqueness for the company and synergy for the general business contour of Syngenta? - In the US market, we have historically had a fairly strong presence in the digital technology segment.  There we have a platform called AgriEdge.  And, of course, we would like to have the same strong presence in Brazil as in the United States.  Accordingly, Strider is a Brazilian company, a digital platform with an already very strong presence there.  Just like Cropio we bought to strengthen its position in Russia and, in general, in Eastern Europe. - But Cropio in Russia is almost not represented.  I think there is a small office, and that ’ s it. – Yes, maybe it is, but the platform has a huge potential and scope for scaling.  It is very important to keep in mind that Cropio has a professional team, and when integrating their platform and their team with our growth opportunities opens up very large ones.  And another strong point of Cropio is that the application in the form in which it is already available can be widely used in Russia.  You were right to say that Cropio has a limited team here.  So if you combine the Cropio software with the large team of sales managers that are in the Russian Syngenta, if you even slightly modify the platform, then there will be very great opportunities. - Are there any calculated figures on the timing, volume of space that you plan to take Cropio services in Russia? - Of course.  At the time of purchase of the service in 2019, Cropio ’ s coverage in Russia was already about 2 million hectares.  In the near future, our goal is to increase this figure to 5 million hectares.  Cropio is a tool that creates additional value for agricultural producers, and it will successfully integrate with the model of creating demand that Syngenta has in Russia.  These are people, a lot of people who will be able to use Cropio and continue to distribute this system. – I understand correctly that your future plant of the SZR near Lipetsk is a tolling model, and there will be no full-fledged localization? – We use the tolling scheme for a very long time, and we will continue to use it in the same place as now – at the Kirovo-Chepetsk Chemical Plant.  But at the same time in Lipetsk we will have our own form, our own packaging of products.  That is, there will be the same process as in Kirovo-Chepetsk.  - Then what is the fundamental difference between what is and what will be? - We see a great prospect of market growth in Russia, we see the opportunity to produce products closer to the client in the Central Black Earth region.  Therefore, we have a lot of flexibility in responding to customer requests.  At the same time, we see great opportunities for exporting our products from this new plant to the EurAsEC countries.  Syngenta.  The producer of seeds and agrochemicals was founded in 2000 on the basis of the agricultural divisions of Novartis and AstraZeneca.  In 2016, it was 100% acquired by the Chinese chemical state corporation ChemChina.  Headquartered in Basel, Switzerland.  It has offices in 90 + countries of the world.  The staff is 28,000 people.  Revenue in 2019 is $13.6 billion (unchanged from 2018), EBITDA is $2.9 billion ($2.7 billion in 2018), net income is $1.45 billion against $1.44 billion a year earlier.  Two-thirds of the company's sales in monetary terms (more than $10 billion) accounted for agrochemicals, a third ($3 billion with a little) - for seeds.  Data on Russia is not disclosed.  Based on Eric Firvald ’ s estimate of Syngenta ’ s 3% share of Russian sales made in this interview, in terms of money they could be at $520 million per year.  Question to you as CEO of the company.  How can you articulate the essence of the new strategy of the company in Russia, which was publicly announced in 2019? - Our strategy in Russia is to be the leader in the segment of crop protection, strengthen our leadership position in sunflower seeds and reach the first place in sales of corn seeds and vegetable crops.  And we want to achieve this by bringing the best world technologies to the Russian market, having high-quality production of the best quality and at the same time providing comprehensive agronomic support with the help of our sales managers and our distribution partners

Title: In the North Caucasus and southern Russia will increase snowfall and droughts
Content: Climatologists predict that in the 21st century, the amount and intensity of snowfall will increase throughout Russia, and in some regions, arid conditions are expected to worsen.  This is reported by RIA Novosti with reference to the national report “Global climate and soil cover of Russia: assessment of risks and environmental and economic consequences of land degradation ”.  The study was conducted with the aim of developing measures for adapting agricultural and forest management systems and technologies to climate change.  Discussion of the report, analyzing the forecast scenarios of climate change and their impact on agriculture and forestry, was held at the Vasily Dokuchaev Soil Institute.  According to scientists, if at the beginning of the XXI century in Russia there was a small increase in precipitation, then by the middle of the century it will increase, especially in the eastern and northern regions of the country.  “The increase in summer precipitation is most significant, mainly in the north and east of Russia.  In the south of the European part of Russia - in the Southern and North Caucasus Federal Districts - the worsening of arid (on average per year) conditions is expected, "the study says.  At the same time, more "sharp" precipitation will probably occur in the form of separate showers or snowfalls.  There will also be more floods and floods.  Note that recently, scientists said that in 30 years the climate of the Rostov region in 30 years may change to subtropical, and the weather on the coast of the Sea of Azov will be close to the climate of Abkhazia and Sochi.  So far, we are lagging behind in temperatures: in the subtropics, the annual is + 11, we have + 9.95, - said Lyudmila Bespalova, Doctor of Geographical Sciences.  In her opinion, the summer shallowing of the Don in 2017, when the water left the coast by ten meters, is one of the brightest examples of climate change.  Changes in climatic conditions can lead not only to a change in flora and fauna, but also to a change in the economy of the region.  For example, Don farmers will have to breed new varieties of wheat and shift the timing of crops.

Title: Land abuse contributes to climate change
Content: The land is often abused and contributes to the harm of climate change 2019-08-06 16: 42 Taiwan Awakening News reporter Zhuang Ruimeng / Taipei reported that the land has been used by humans to cultivate and lose its original function of absorbing carbon.  (Photo by M. Prinke on Flicker under Creative Commons license) Share Facebook Treating land better helps humanity fight climate change.  The UN Intergovernmental Panel of Experts on Climate Change, which is currently meeting, will present an updated report on the current state of human land use.  Experts pointed out that due to human behavior, land has changed from carbon capture to carbon release, threatening to exacerbate the power of climate change, and highlighting the importance of land use.  According to The Independent, global soils can currently absorb 1% of carbon, down from 7% in the past.  If the land is cultivated in a more sustainable way, carbon will be absorbed by the soil to become a carbon reservoir.  Currently, 1 / 3 of all pollution emissions come from land.  “If we take the severity of the climate problem seriously now, it will be worse if we don ’ t have land as a carbon reservoir, ” said Li Wen, a representative of the World Resources Institute. The scientists also pointed out that continued pressure on land, including the provision of food, wood and plant raw materials to meet increasing population needs, will make carbon reduction targets more difficult to achieve.  In addition, 33% of arable land has been used to grow crops that provide animal feed.  Professor Lixon of the University of Clanfield in the UK also believes that the latest IPCC report will provide more evidence that land degradation will also exacerbate climate change and lead to an increase in the crisis.  Addressing land abuse can focus on intensive agriculture, which involves farming on as small a land as possible, allowing more natural land to absorb carbon dioxide, according to the BBC.  Another option is to farm in a less dense and friendly climate.  Either way, however, the IPCC report will point out that poor farmers will be the group most affected by global warming.  Professor Berman, of the University of Oxford ’ s Institute of Environmental Change, said climate change had led to soil erosion in the south of the UK through more intense rainfall.  “Warmer temperatures and heavier rainfall will worsen soil erosion, soil compaction, loss of organic matter and biodiversity, and soil and rock flows, ” said Li Huicheng, chairman of the IPCC.“ I hope this report will serve to remind the world more about the threat that climate change poses to land. ”  [More details, see here]

Title: Climate change and water scarcity are top priorities.
Content: Assistant Professor of Water Engineering at the Faculty of Agriculture of Shahrekord University said: “The main priority of the authorities should be water shortage and climate change, so that water factories are moved to the seaside and agriculture in areas that are facing water shortage is limited. ”  He said: “It ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time, it ’ s been a long time.  “When we talk about climate change, we mean meteorological parameters that have been measured over long periods of time, and these changes manifest themselves in either natural or artificial forms, which are caused by humans.  Nasr Esfahani said: “Various factors such as sunspots, changes in the earth ’ s crust, changes in vegetation or the movement of continents, or changes in ocean temperature naturally cause climate change.  “What has happened in the past year is that humans have caused an imbalance in meteorological parameters due to excessive consumption of natural resources, including oil, gas and fossil fuels, and by destroying natural resources such as forests and expanding factories and cities.  The university professor pointed out that the country is climatally located in a dry region, saying: "We should not expect the climate to change from dry to wet, because this is a very wrong expectation that some in the society suggest this."  He said: "Climate change has become very clear in the last 40 years, so we have to adapt to this situation that has been fluctuating and know that drought or drought fluctuations are part of the nature of the region's climate."  Nasr Isfahani said: "In this situation, climate change is occurring and extreme phenomena such as severe droughts, drought, heat and cold are increasing, there is no alternative but to adapt to them, for example, agricultural products can be used to prevent frostbite, to use resistant products.  Regarding water resources, he said: “At the same time as the climate change, the consumption of water resources has greatly expanded, especially in the last 50 years, when agriculture has been the center of development in the country. ”  The university professor said: "If we examine the rainfall parameter in more detail, we see that the average rainfall has not changed, but the extremes have changed a lot and these changes are significant, on the other hand, the effective rainfall has not changed and the ineffective rainfall has increased, which means that there is a shortage of water resources."  He said: "What has been observed is that, contrary to the rainfall parameter, changes in the temperature parameter, especially the minimum temperature, are highly effective and the trend of increasing the minimum temperature is observed in many stations in the country."  Nasr Esfahani pointed out that in mountainous areas the precipitation has changed from solid to liquid state, adding: "When there is snow in the region, because the snow is slowly melting and sinking into underground sources, it feeds them, on the other hand, the occurrence of rain brings water runoff, which feeds surface water instead of feeding groundwater resources."  He added that excessive consumption of water resources, expansion of the area under cultivation, non-observance of the cultivation pattern and the use of traditional methods for irrigation have led to the reduction of groundwater.  Assistant Professor of Water Engineering at Shahrekord University emphasized: "The authorities were aware of the current situation, but they did not think that the effects of climate change would be egregious and misrepresented, and today we face a fundamental problem, for example, if there was a shortage of water, it was solved by harvesting from underground water resources and we assigned this problem to the future."  He continued: “We have reached a point where groundwater resources are not the answer to the shortage of water, and this problem has become such that measures must be taken.  Nasr Esfahani said that for short-term purposes, water resources have not been considered because steel and water mills have been built in the country, which if this decision process continues, despite the lack of water resources, will still be built in the future.  “We should not expect that one day our country will be as abundant as Europe, because the lack of rainfall in our region has been caused by the rotation of the earth and the circulation of the atmosphere, so in addition to adapting to climate change, if there is to be a cost to this, it should be done today and we should not postpone those costs to the future, because we may face more limitations in the future. ”  The university professor noted that the main priority of the authorities should be water scarcity and climate change, so that water factories are moved to the seaside and agriculture is limited in areas with water scarcity.  End of message.

Title: Climate change and 21% reduction in agricultural productivity
Content: In a new study led by Cornell University in the US, experts have found that farms have averaged 21 percent less yields over the past six decades as a result of climate change.  According to the researchers, this equates to a total loss of seven years of agricultural productivity growth.  Global agriculture is increasingly exposed to the effects of climate change, with warmer places such as Africa and Latin America suffering the most, and agricultural productivity growth is currently down by 34%.  To quantify the impact of human-induced climate change on what economists call “total factor productivity or a measure of overall agricultural sector productivity, ” experts developed a comprehensive econometric model.  Professor Robert Chambers, from the University of Maryland, said the results show that climate-related factors have already had a major impact on agricultural productivity.  In this paper, we used a model to estimate how the total factor productivity patterns would be if climate change were not present.  Professor Ariel Ortiz Boba, principal investigator of the study and assistant professor at Cornell University ’ s School of Applied Economics and Management, said: “We found that climate change has wiped out about seven years of progress in agricultural productivity over the past 60 years, equating to pressing the stop button for productivity growth in 2013, after which no progress has been made, and now human climate change is slowing down.  According to Professor Ortiz Boba, the group considered more than 200 systematic changes from the econometric model, and the results were largely consistent.  When we focus on different regions of the world, we find that the historical impacts of climate change have been greatest in areas that have become warmer, including areas of Africa, Latin America and Asia.  Most people see climate change as a distant problem, but it ’ s one that ’ s already having an impact.  We need to address climate change now so that we can prevent future generations from being harmed.  The study was published in the journal Nature Climate Change.  End of message.

Title: What is the origin of the food crisis in Latin America?
Content: According to the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) website, the Latin American and Caribbean region produces enough food to meet the needs of all its inhabitants.  So the main problem with hunger in the region is not the lack of food, but the obstacles and difficulties faced by the poor to obtain it.  FAO Deputy General and Representative of the Organization for Latin America Julio Bardege told DW on the occasion of World Food Day that hunger in Latin America is due to insufficient income and significant economic inequality, which afflicts millions of people in the region.  According to a new report by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), food prices remained high for a seventh consecutive month in the last month of 2020, with dairy products and vegetable oils driving the biggest price increases.  According to the FAO, the rise in food prices was due to higher demand and weaker dollar values.  According to experts, although there is no pressure on food shortages, the impact of the epidemic on the supply chain and the restriction of traffic has caused damage to farms.  Latin America and the Caribbean, which produce more than 14 percent of the world ’ s food, are also looking to reshape their farming arrangements to feed 10 billion people by 2050.  However, the COVID-19 epidemic has caused an unprecedented setback in the region ’ s struggle against hunger, adding more than 20 million people to the ranks of poverty.  The unprecedented health crisis that has plagued the world for nearly two years has also hit Latin America.  Latin America, which was among the most vulnerable regions in the world due to the epidemic, has seen the spread of poverty and food shortages in recent decades, not only due to the spread of the coronavirus and the increase in deaths caused by it, but also due to numerous other factors such as climate change, mismanagement and the increasing deterioration of the labor market and sanctions.  The epidemic puts 45 million people in Latin America in a state of absolute poverty.  A situation that has sounded warnings and alarms about the lack of social security networks to reduce the consequences of the epidemic in Latin America.  The NGO Action Against Hunger reported a three-fold increase in the number of people suffering from food insecurity in Latin America in 2020 due to the outbreak of COVID-19.  In Peru, 80 percent of people lost their jobs or their incomes dropped by an average of 33 percent, according to the Humanitarian Institute ’ s survey.  The 20% drop in global food production due to climate change is another crisis that experts have warned of.  Studies show that climate change has reduced global food production by more than 20 percent in the past 60 years.  Farmers have one-fifth less food than they had in 1961; in warmer regions such as Latin America and Africa, the decline is up to 34 percent.  According to available data, the United States only sees growth of 5 to 15 percent, while the world's population is projected to reach 10 billion by 2050.  Climate change has changed the favorable conditions for growing crops and is hurting the food chain in the future.  Experts believe that temperature in plant growth and development is one of the important factors.  Temperature, along with the surface of light; carbon dioxide, temperature humidity, water and nutrients, affect the growth and ultimately the production of crops.  All of these factors need to be balanced.  While the global population continues to rise, a new study suggests that agricultural productivity has fallen sharply due to the effects of climate change.  On the other hand, some coercive measures by the hegemonic powers against the countries of the Latin American resistance, such as Venezuela, have exacerbated the food crisis in the region.  Along with mismanagement of the country ’ s food security, the impact of sanctions has affected 96 percent of Venezuelans, according to a new study.  The region ’ s response to the epidemic of the Director General of the Latin American Regional Agricultural Organization has increased despite the region ’ s worsening agricultural export unemployment during the epidemic.  In response to COVID-19 pandemic, the director of the Food and Agriculture Organization has sought to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of food production with a strategic approach, and has made a huge change in the agricultural sector with new regional initiatives.  The senior official of the agricultural organization of the region also emphasized the need for large-scale investments, especially in supply chain infrastructure and agricultural innovations, expressed hope about the region ’ s significant capacities, such as the enormous natural resources of the region, abundance of fresh water and fertile lands, as well as diverse ecosystems.  Despite this, the devastating effects of the epidemic will continue to plague the Latin American region.  Predictably, in most of these countries, rising debt due to the injection of emergency funds into the health sector and the provision of direct assistance to affected families and industrial sectors affected by the recession reduced economic activity by 7.7% in 2020.  The unemployment rate, which is the main cause of poverty, increased by 2.6 percent and with a significant portion of the workforce leaving, it reached 10.7 percent from its previous year in 2019.  In the same vein, because it was not possible for many jobs to work remotely, only 21.3 percent of those employed in the Latin American region were able to continue working this way.  According to the study, the highest unemployment rate was found in Peru (39.5%), Argentina (20.9%), Colombia (21.8%), Costa Rica (20.1%), and in the poorest households, informal work dominated.  According to the website Wordo Mitters, more than 33,581 million people in Latin America and the Caribbean have been infected with the coronavirus, and more than 1.2 million people have died from the disease.

Title: Infographic Understanding Climate Change: Warmer weather not only harms human health, but agriculture and the economy have also paid the price
Content: David Nelles and Christian Serrer: Climate change has now directly or indirectly affected the lives of 7.5 billion people on the planet.  However, the impact of global warming varies from place to place, which means that people and people living together in different regions will also be affected to varying degrees.  In any case, one thing is certain: the continued warming of the climate will continue to bring all kinds of adverse effects to mankind.  Climate change can have many effects on human health, such as heat stress caused by high temperature, operating environment factors (including air temperature, humidity, wind speed and radiation heat) and clothing, and high temperature events, which can worsen heart, blood circulation and respiratory related diseases. Increase the mortality rate of these diseases.  On the other hand, high temperatures are conducive to the formation of ozone close to the ground, which has adverse effects on human health, such as may lead to decreased lung function.  Extreme weather events such as floods or storms are more frequent and can also bring more hidden risks to human health, such as injuries and even death in serious cases.  In addition, already polluted waters may increase the risk of infectious disease outbreaks due to heavy rainfall and flooding.  Another effect of climate change in Germany is the lengthening of the pollen season, which exacerbates the symptoms of respiratory diseases such as asthma or allergic rhinitis.  And such climatic conditions are more conducive to the growth and reproduction of allergenic plants, such as Ambrosia is a good example.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse Produced The 2010 increase in global deaths due to climate change A spreading vector of disease caused by climate change refers to organisms that can transmit pathogens from infected animals or humans to other animals or humans, such as ticks commonly known as ticks, or mosquitoes.  Climate change is changing the current environmental conditions in which pathogens are spread by vectors.  In recent decades, due to globalization and favorable climatic conditions, the Asian-native Aedes albopictus (also known as the Asian tiger mosquito) has reached parts of southern Europe.  In the near future, other areas of higher latitudes in Europe should also become suitable for mosquito activity due to climate change.  It is important to note that the white line mosquito spreads dengue fever and Chikungunya virus.  On the other hand, the high temperature must be maintained for a period of time before the virus can be spread through the infected mosquitoes, because the warm temperature allows the virus to successfully reproduce in the mosquitoes and then transmit the virus to humans when the mosquitoes bite.  Rising temperatures create favorable conditions for the spread of Aedes albopictus and shorten the propagation time of the virus in Aedes albopictus.  Combining globalization with the risks that come with it, such as the importation of foreign goods that could trap Aedes albopictus, or returning travelers infected with the virus, increases the risk of disease transmission.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produce Climate change impacts on agriculture High temperatures, high levels of carbon dioxide in the air, changes in rainfall patterns, and associated changing weather parameters can affect plant growth.  When the temperature rises to the most appropriate growth temperature, the yield of a particular crop can be increased, but once the temperature exceeds this optimum value, the crop yield begins to decrease.  In the case of corn and soybeans, as long as the growth period is more than 30 ° C, it is not conducive to the development of these crops.  In addition, extreme weather, especially drought and high temperatures, as well as heavy rain, can negatively affect yields. Between 2000 and 2007 alone, droughts and high temperatures have reduced global cereal crops by about 6.2%.  When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air increases, many plants respond quickly by reducing the amount of water released from the leaves and increasing photosynthesis.  In this way, there is enough water and nutrients to promote plant growth, which is known as the "CO2 fertilization effect" (CO2-Düngungseffekt).  There is debate as to how much this fertilization effect can offset the reduction in production in some areas due to changes in temperature and rainfall patterns.  In addition, increased carbon dioxide concentration in the air can promote plant growth, but it also means that the nutrient concentration in the plant will be relatively reduced.  If higher average temperatures lead to longer tillage periods, less cold damage and higher crop yields, then climate change has positive implications for higher latitudes, such as northern Europe.  In contrast, climate change is not necessarily a good thing for crop yields in tropical and subtropical regions.  Climate change comes with three different types of costs: First, the cost of damage, such as direct damage to real estate or public infrastructure caused by extreme weather events.  This is followed by adaptation costs, such as levees or ponds for flood control.  The third is the so-called avoidance costs, such as the costs of switching from fossil to renewable energy to limit future global warming.  Because it is not possible to have a clear and comprehensive picture of all the costs incurred, it is actually very difficult to calculate precise figures for the economic costs of climate change.  Therefore, the calculated cost can only depend on the assumptions made, and it is very difficult to accurately grasp the costs of such things, such as melted permafrost, so it is extremely difficult to analyze the chart below.  Photo Credit: Business Week Publishing / Produced by Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse Because of these high levels of uncertainty, it is very difficult to know exactly what climate protection measures should be taken and how much it should be interfered with from a purely economic point of view.  If people want to limit warming to 1.5 ° C, they will have to pay a very high investment cost.  Compared to setting the temperature rise range at a maximum of 3.5 ° C, the investment cost, although significantly reduced, will result in higher damage costs.  Overall, the cost of limiting global warming should be much less than the cost of damage caused by an unrestricted rise in global temperatures.  It is worth noting that as the temperature rises, the risk of irreversible damage is also increased.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse conclude that climate change is not a distant vision of the future, and that it represents more than just melting icebergs and rising sea levels, which are already threatening many people and their livelihoods.  In addition, it also shows that the temperature rise observed since the beginning of the industrial era is mainly due to man-made greenhouse gas emissions.  Fortunately, there ’ s also some ironic good news: we have the opportunity to influence the future of the climate, and we ’ re not completely powerless against climate change!  Climate model simulations show that as long as humans reduce greenhouse gas emissions, it is expected to limit the development of global warming.  Photo Credit: Businessweek / Lisa Schwegler, Stefan Kraiss, and Janna Geisse produced a global average temperature forecast for greenhouse gas emissions, but since the United Nations Climate Conference (UN-Klimakonferenz) was first held in Berlin in 1995, global greenhouse gas emissions have risen by 50%, reaching a record high.  If human beings continue to produce large quantities of greenhouse gases, it is not impossible to imagine that global temperatures will rise by another 5 ° C by the end of the century.  Therefore, we must all be aware of our responsibility: how the future of the climate, and the extent to which the impact of global warming will worsen, is entirely in our hands! Title: Tyumen scientists conduct observations at the biological station "Lake Kuchak"
Content: Tyumen scientists conduct observations at the biological station "Lake Kuchak" | Photo: Tyumen State University | Photo: Tyumen State University Regular observations of the growth and development of various field crops, taking into account the impact on plants of meteorological factors on the experimental site of the biological station of Tyumen State University "Lake Kuchak" are carried out by scientists of the Institute of Biology of Tyumen State University since May 2020, according to the Department of Strategic Communications of the university.  The territory is a natural testing ground for the study of ecological plasticity of plants and the selection of forms with high adaptive potential.  As explained by the head of the Department of Botany, Biotechnology and Landscape Architecture of Tyumen State University, Professor Nina Bome, the growing season of 2020 is characterized by an extremely uneven distribution in time of precipitation and air temperature.  Drought-resistant forms of cultivated plants that have the ability to adapt to the temperature stresses of the environment acquire practical value.  The success of the introduction of cultivated species can be achieved only with the right selection of varieties and the development of elements of regional cultivation technology.  In this regard, plant forms created by scientists of the Institute of Biology with the help of modern genetic and biotechnological methods are of particular value: chemical mutagenesis, hybridization, selection.  In total, about 800 experimental variants of the genetic diversity of cultivated plants were included in the research.  Some research projects are carried out in partnership with scientific and educational Russian and foreign centers.

Title: Climate Change Impact Assessment on Taiwan ’ s Human Resources (Part I)
Content: Rising temperatures, intense heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rain are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Pixabay economic growth is engulfed if we do not make substantial and sustained global mitigation of climate change, and regional adaptation efforts, it is expected to cost us infrastructure and property, increasingly, and hinder economic growth.  In the absence of major global mitigation actions and regional adaptation efforts, rising temperatures, rising sea levels and changes in extreme weather will continue to destroy infrastructure and property, labor productivity, and community vitality, especially as regional economies and industries that rely on natural resources and climate-friendly conditions, such as agriculture, tourism, and fisheries, are increasingly vulnerable to climate change.  Rising temperatures are expected to reduce the efficiency of power generation and increase energy demand, which in turn increases the cost of electricity.  Climate change is also expected to increasingly affect trade and the economy, including import and export prices, as well as businesses with overseas operations and supply chains.  In a moderately warm world, some aspects of the economy may improve slightly in the short term.  However, if the world does not reduce greenhouse gas emissions significantly and continuously, the planet is expected to continue to warm, causing significant net damage to the economy this century, especially as adaptation efforts are thwarted.  It is expected that the annual losses in some sectors of the economy will reach hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the century, continuing to grow at the rate of past emissions.  Agriculture is highly challenged and threatened by rising temperatures, heat, drought, orchard burning and heavy rains, which are expected to increasingly undermine agricultural productivity.  Challenges to livestock health, expected increases, declining crop yields and quality, and changes in extreme weather threaten rural livelihoods, food security, and price stability.  Climate change poses many challenges to maintaining and improving crop productivity, livestock health and the economic viability of rural communities.  While some regions may see gains in productivity favoring expanded or alternative crops in the coming decades, overall, production of major crops is expected to decline due to higher temperatures, potentially altering water availability, soil erosion, and outbreaks of disease and pests.  Rising temperatures during the growing season are expected to be the biggest factor in the decline in agricultural productivity.  If the temperature at night exceeds 35 ° C, it will cause rice to be unable to pollinate; it will also aggravate the impact of diseases and pests, affecting the harvest of crops; high temperature and rain will make the soil unable to maintain nutrients, reduce crop yields and increase production costs.  The expected increase in extreme hot weather is expected to result in further heat stress for livestock, resulting in significant economic losses for producers.  Climate change is also likely to cause large-scale changes in the supply and prices of many agricultural products around the world, and the global supply and prices of agricultural products will also change dramatically.  These changes threaten future gains in commodity crop production and endanger rural livelihoods.  Agricultural production is an industry that is highly dependent on natural resources such as water, soil and biodiversity.  Climate change causes global temperature increases and uneven rainfall, disrupting crop growth, affecting the original habitats of ecosystems, and affecting the yield and quality of agricultural products, endangering food security and productivity, and causing loss of biodiversity.  There are many adaptation strategies to cope with climate variability, while reversing the adverse effects of change on agricultural production.  These include changes in production content, production inputs, the adoption of new technologies, and changes in management principles.  However, these strategies have limitations under severe climate change impacts and require both long-term and short-term investments.  High risk to health Climate change Air quality and health risks from extreme weather, air quality, and insects and pests, diseases transmitted through food and water supplies, are increasingly threatening the health and well-being of already vulnerable people; changes in temperature and precipitation increase air quality and health risks from wildfires (or incineration) and ground ozone pollution; rising air and water temperatures and more intense extreme weather are expected to increase exposure to waterborne diseases and foodborne diseases (food Sexual diseases), affecting the safety of food and water supplies.  Due to climate change, the frequency and severity of allergic diseases, including asthma and pollen fever, are expected to increase.  It also changes and expands the geographical distribution of disease-carrying insects and pests, exposing more people to the lice that bring Lyme disease and the mosquitoes that transmit Zika virus (such as dengue, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis and Nile virus), which affect different transregions.  For example, communities in southwestern Taiwan are particularly vulnerable to the combined health effects of vector-borne diseases and high temperatures and floods.  Extreme and climate-related weather can have lasting mental health effects on communities, with adverse consequences, in particular resulting in degradation of livelihoods or relocation of communities.  Including the elderly, children, people in low-income communities and some indigenous and new communities, they tend to be disproportionately affected by the health impacts of climate change and are less resilient.  This helps individuals, communities, and counties to prepare for climate change risks with policies and programs to adapt and mitigate to reduce the number of injuries, illnesses, and deaths from adverse health outcomes.  According to the study, if the average temperature in Taiwan increases by 1 ° C in the future, the high risk of dengue fever will increase to 86, affecting more than 7 million people. In addition, the number of medium-risk areas has also increased to 203, and the future warming status will significantly increase the prevalence of dengue fever in Taiwan.  In addition, the increase in temperature in Taiwan will also increase the risk of related infectious diseases, and the impact of rainfall changes on infectious diseases will be more significant when the "daily extreme rainfall" is greater than 200mm.  In the face of the impact of climate change on public health, the adaptation that must be considered and prepared can be classified as at least three major aspects of infectious diseases, chronic non-communicable diseases and emergency medical care.  The main adjustment policies can basically be considered from the angle of strengthening and prevention.

Title: Eric Firvald, Syngenta. “Climate change will be a major global factor ”
Content: — More than two years ago, we met at SPIEF — shortly after the closing of the deal with ChemChina.  You said then that this is the optimal shareholder, which will preserve the independence of the company, including the operating one.  It's been a while.  Can you say the same now?  I would like to draw your attention to the fact that outside of China the influence of our shareholders is quite limited.  The only thing they can do is support us, including investment.  Support is coming!  We have made five acquisitions, including our largest acquisition of Nidera, the digital platform Cropio, two deals in the vegetable segment and one in the digital tools segment.  There is also support from shareholders.  Let ’ s say in China, they help us to better understand the local market in order to improve the service of Chinese customers.  Historically, there have been problems in China with the use of low-quality pesticides, overuse of pesticides, low-quality fertilizers...  As a result, this has led to soil degradation and environmental problems.  Accordingly, with the new Chinese shareholder, we have the opportunity to increase our share in the Chinese market, while bringing our high-quality modern products to it and thereby help the country overcome the difficulties that it has. - How has your share in the Chinese market increased since the transaction? - We have significantly increased it.  We had less than 1% of the market in China and 6% in the crop.  By the end of last year, we already had 4% for seeds and 10% of the crop protection market.  If we talk about the implementation, then by the end of 2019, our sales in China amounted to $336 million.  By the end of 2020, our sales in China will exceed $4 billion, and the market share will increase significantly.  Eric Firvald.  CEO Syngenta was born on July 29, 1959 in the United States.  1981 – Graduated from the University of Delaware (Chemical Engineering).  1998 — studied in the program of training of top managers of Harvard Business School.  2003 - Vice President, Agriculture and Nutrition, DuPont Group.  2008 — Chairman of the Board of Directors, President and CEO at Nalco (water treatment technologies, services for energy companies).  2011 — President of EcoLab (water, hygiene and energy technologies and services).  2012 — Executive Director of Univar (world distributor of chemical products, including agricultural products).  Since 2016 — CEO of Syngenta. — Tell us the details of the transactions. — Nidera is a company that deals with corn and soybean seeds, one of the largest players of this level in Brazil and Argentina.  And, of course, integration with the Syngenta business turns the now merged company Syngenta-Nidera into one of the leading market makers in the markets of these countries.  With the acquisition of Nidera, we also gained access to advanced technologies in the field of sunflower and, by the way, these technologies will soon be available in Russia.  The second two important acquisitions are the digital platforms Cropio and Strider.  Digital platforms help to keep a record of the use of all those crop protection products and fertilizers used by the agricultural producer, and give him certain advice.  In this way, they help us to improve our customer service.  Among our deals are two more seed companies in the vegetable segment: Abbott & Cobb and Floranova.  These companies are mainly represented in the markets of the United States and the United Kingdom, but their hermoplasm is used far beyond these countries. – Name, if possible, the amount of each of the transactions. – This I can not do.  I will only say that all five acquisitions cost the company and its shareholders $2 billion. — Can an M & A deal similar to one of these five be concluded in Russia? — I will say at once that Chinese investors fully support our course to increase investment in Russian business.  But here we have a few other plans.  When I talk about Russia, I mean, first of all, not M & A, but the construction of a plant for the production of plant protection products near Lipetsk and the creation of the Institute for Seed Protection in the Voronezh region, which will support our business in this segment.  We also intend to significantly increase the number of full-time employees in Russia. - And how much does Russia occupy in your sales? - 4%, but at the same time we maintain a constant increase in sales here.  Of course, its pace is not as fast as in China, but our starting positions in the two countries are different. – Another question about the new digital assets of Syngenta.  The Cropio platform is relatively known in Russia, and almost nothing is known about Strider.  What is this platform where it works, what is its uniqueness for the company and synergy for the general business contour of Syngenta? - In the US market, we have historically had a fairly strong presence in the digital technology segment.  There we have a platform called AgriEdge.  And, of course, we would like to have the same strong presence in Brazil as in the United States.  Accordingly, Strider is a Brazilian company, a digital platform with an already very strong presence there.  Just like Cropio we bought to strengthen its position in Russia and, in general, in Eastern Europe. - But Cropio in Russia is almost not represented.  I think there is a small office, and that ’ s it. – Yes, maybe it is, but the platform has a huge potential and scope for scaling.  It is very important to keep in mind that Cropio has a professional team, and when integrating their platform and their team with our growth opportunities opens up very large ones.  And another strong point of Cropio is that the application in the form in which it is already available can be widely used in Russia.  You were right to say that Cropio has a limited team here.  So if you combine the Cropio software with the large team of sales managers that are in the Russian Syngenta, if you even slightly modify the platform, then there will be very great opportunities. - Are there any calculated figures on the timing, volume of space that you plan to take Cropio services in Russia? - Of course.  At the time of purchase of the service in 2019, Cropio ’ s coverage in Russia was already about 2 million hectares.  In the near future, our goal is to increase this figure to 5 million hectares.  Cropio is a tool that creates additional value for agricultural producers, and it will successfully integrate with the model of creating demand that Syngenta has in Russia.  These are people, a lot of people who will be able to use Cropio and continue to distribute this system. – I understand correctly that your future plant of the SZR near Lipetsk is a tolling model, and there will be no full-fledged localization? – We use the tolling scheme for a very long time, and we will continue to use it in the same place as now – at the Kirovo-Chepetsk Chemical Plant.  But at the same time in Lipetsk we will have our own form, our own packaging of products.  That is, there will be the same process as in Kirovo-Chepetsk.  - Then what is the fundamental difference between what is and what will be? - We see a great prospect of market growth in Russia, we see the opportunity to produce products closer to the client in the Central Black Earth region.  Therefore, we have a lot of flexibility in responding to customer requests.  At the same time, we see great opportunities for exporting our products from this new plant to the EurAsEC countries.  Syngenta.  The producer of seeds and agrochemicals was founded in 2000 on the basis of the agricultural divisions of Novartis and AstraZeneca.  In 2016, it was 100% acquired by the Chinese chemical state corporation ChemChina.  Headquartered in Basel, Switzerland.  It has offices in 90 + countries of the world.  The staff is 28,000 people.  Revenue in 2019 is $13.6 billion (unchanged from 2018), EBITDA is $2.9 billion ($2.7 billion in 2018), net income is $1.45 billion against $1.44 billion a year earlier.  Two-thirds of the company's sales in monetary terms (more than $10 billion) accounted for agrochemicals, a third ($3 billion with a little) - for seeds.  Data on Russia is not disclosed.  Based on Eric Firvald ’ s estimate of Syngenta ’ s 3% share of Russian sales made in this interview, in terms of money they could be at $520 million per year.  Question to you as CEO of the company.  How can you articulate the essence of the new strategy of the company in Russia, which was publicly announced in 2019? - Our strategy in Russia is to be the leader in the segment of crop protection, strengthen our leadership position in sunflower seeds and reach the first place in sales of corn seeds and vegetable crops.  And we want to achieve this by bringing the best world technologies to the Russian market, having high-quality production of the best quality and at the same time providing comprehensive agronomic support with the help of our sales managers and our distribution partners

Title: In the North Caucasus and southern Russia will increase snowfall and droughts
Content: Climatologists predict that in the 21st century, the amount and intensity of snowfall will increase throughout Russia, and in some regions, arid conditions are expected to worsen.  This is reported by RIA Novosti with reference to the national report “Global climate and soil cover of Russia: assessment of risks and environmental and economic consequences of land degradation ”.  The study was conducted with the aim of developing measures for adapting agricultural and forest management systems and technologies to climate change.  Discussion of the report, analyzing the forecast scenarios of climate change and their impact on agriculture and forestry, was held at the Vasily Dokuchaev Soil Institute.  According to scientists, if at the beginning of the XXI century in Russia there was a small increase in precipitation, then by the middle of the century it will increase, especially in the eastern and northern regions of the country.  “The increase in summer precipitation is most significant, mainly in the north and east of Russia.  In the south of the European part of Russia - in the Southern and North Caucasus Federal Districts - the worsening of arid (on average per year) conditions is expected, "the study says.  At the same time, more "sharp" precipitation will probably occur in the form of separate showers or snowfalls.  There will also be more floods and floods.  Note that recently, scientists said that in 30 years the climate of the Rostov region in 30 years may change to subtropical, and the weather on the coast of the Sea of Azov will be close to the climate of Abkhazia and Sochi.  So far, we are lagging behind in temperatures: in the subtropics, the annual is + 11, we have + 9.95, - said Lyudmila Bespalova, Doctor of Geographical Sciences.  In her opinion, the summer shallowing of the Don in 2017, when the water left the coast by ten meters, is one of the brightest examples of climate change.  Changes in climatic conditions can lead not only to a change in flora and fauna, but also to a change in the economy of the region.  For example, Don farmers will have to breed new varieties of wheat and shift the timing of crops.
